Hello, welcome all Chuds, Gamers, and other Nerds. I aim to 100% all the games that catch my eye and join the sea of reviews on this platform.
Most will never read this, but I will review the games I find simply and thoroughly.

(Note: This is a copy of my Bioshock Remaster review, in which I have 100%ed the game for those who may judge this based off of playtime. This was simple stability testing in comparison with the Remaster.) 

1 What is Bioshock?
Bioshock takes place in Rapture, a underwater utopia located under the Atlantic ocean. When you discover this city after a plane crash, Rapture has become a hellscape. You are now forced to survive it in your efforts to escape, and you will find yourself wrapped in a conspiracy.

2 What does this game play like?
This game was inspired off of System Shock and would later inspire other immersive sims like Arkane studios Dishonored. As a result of this games inspiration, Bioshock is a first person shooter that relies on environmental interaction and impact. You can shoot lightening from your hand, shoot it into water, and everything in the water will get hurt, fire melts ice, and so on and so on. The gun play is also satisfying, not relying on typical COD hide and shoot game play, but more on positioning to use the environment against your foes.

Simple rankings
Story 10/10: This game is known for it's story, and it is a masterpiece. Bioshock examines themes from the real life Ann Rand, but it is not just limited by her rejection of government, but it also examines human nature regarding the idea of a utopia. Did Rapture fail because anarcho capitalism is fundamentally flawed? Or did it fail because Andrew Ryan became what he hated most, a government more controlling than NZ Germany or the Soviet Union? Would you kindly just play it?

Game play 10/10: The game play is well paced and immersive. Each of the zones has a theme and grants you the freedom to use all your tools to overcome your opponents. Each map has plenty to explore and interact with, for a immersive sim, the only better game you will find is Dishonored 1.

Overall 10/10: This fits into the immersive sim genera as one of the greats, a masterpiece one could say, and it earns the 10/10 reputation it has.

BioShock Review: Ambitious, Atmospheric, Slightly Uneven

BioShock (2007), developed by Irrational Games, is a first-person shooter that stands out for its strong narrative and striking setting. Set in the underwater city of Rapture, the game mixes dystopian storytelling with action-heavy gameplay, though not always seamlessly.

Narrative & Setting:
The story is its biggest strength, exploring themes like free will and the dangers of unchecked ambition. Rapture itself is richly designed, its Art Deco visuals and ruined grandeur make it a compelling backdrop. However, some of the philosophical themes can feel heavy-handed or underdeveloped by the end.

Gameplay:
Combat mixes standard gunplay with powers called Plasmids, offering some tactical flexibility. Early encounters feel fresh, but enemy variety and repetitive combat loops can wear thin over time. The hacking mini-game, while initially interesting, becomes tedious after repeated use.

Visuals & Sound:
The atmosphere is excellent, supported by strong art direction and a haunting soundscape. However, some textures and animations show their age. Voice acting is generally solid, though a few supporting characters feel one-dimensional.

Verdict:
BioShock is an ambitious game that succeeds more in atmosphere and storytelling than in mechanics. It's worth playing for its unique world and ideas, even if the gameplay doesn’t always match the narrative’s depth.

"BioShock," developed by Irrational Games and released in 2007, is a first-person shooter that blends innovative gameplay, a compelling narrative, and atmospheric world-building to create a memorable experience. Set in the dystopian underwater city of Rapture, players explore a society that has fallen into ruin, uncovering its secrets and surviving the dangers that lurk within. This review evaluates "BioShock" based on its gameplay mechanics, story and setting, graphical and audio presentation, impact on the gaming industry, and overall entertainment value.

Gameplay Mechanics
Rating: 9/10 - Excellent
"BioShock" stands out for its gameplay mechanics, which expertly combine traditional first-person shooter elements with unique plasmid powers, offering players a wide range of combat strategies. The ability to modify weapons and use environmental hazards against enemies adds depth and variety to encounters. The game also incorporates RPG elements, allowing for character customization through gene upgrades, which enhances the strategic component of gameplay. The innovative use of plasmids and the game's approach to combat and exploration set a new standard for the genre.

Story and Setting
Rating: 10/10 - Masterpiece
The narrative and world of "BioShock" are where the game truly shines. Rapture, with its art deco design and retro-futuristic technology, is a character in its own right, rich with history and mystery. The story, exploring themes of free will, human nature, and the dangers of unchecked ambition, is engaging and thought-provoking. The city's descent into madness is revealed through environmental storytelling and audio diaries, providing a deep and immersive narrative experience that few games have matched.

Graphical and Audio Presentation
Rating: 9/10 - Excellent
At the time of its release, "BioShock" was praised for its stunning visuals, which meticulously captured the eerie beauty and decay of Rapture. The attention to detail in the environment, character models, and visual effects contributes to the game's immersive atmosphere. The audio design, from the haunting soundtrack to the chilling sound effects and voice acting, plays a crucial role in building tension and enhancing the storytelling, making the exploration of Rapture an unforgettable experience.

Impact on the Gaming Industry
Rating: 10/10 - Masterpiece
"BioShock" had a profound impact on the gaming industry, influencing countless games that followed. It demonstrated that video games could be a powerful medium for storytelling, capable of exploring complex themes and presenting players with moral dilemmas. The game's integration of narrative and gameplay, along with its innovative mechanics and atmospheric world-building, have been cited as inspirations by many developers, cementing its legacy as a landmark title in gaming history.

Overall Entertainment Value
Rating: 9/10 - Excellent
"BioShock" offers an exceptional entertainment value, combining a compelling story, engaging gameplay, and a richly detailed world. The game's ability to immerse players in its dystopian underwater setting, challenging them to survive and uncover the truth of Rapture, makes for a captivating experience from start to finish. While some aspects of gameplay may feel dated to players revisiting the game or experiencing it for the first time years after its release, "BioShock" remains a must-play title for its narrative depth and innovative design.

Overall Summary and Score
Overall Rating: 9.4/10 - Masterpiece
"BioShock" is a seminal game that masterfully blends narrative, gameplay, and atmosphere to create an experience that is both thought-provoking and immensely enjoyable. Its impact on the gaming industry and the way stories can be told through interactive media is undeniable, making it not only a landmark title in the first-person shooter genre but also in video gaming as a whole.

Essential for gamers interested in narrative-driven experiences and fans of first-person shooters looking for depth and innovation in gameplay. "BioShock" is a defining game of its generation, offering a rich and immersive journey into the heart of a utopian dream turned nightmare.

This game was supposed to be the spiritual successor to a very powerful game: System Shock 2. The environment and the story are supposed to be dark and horrifying, with every piece you learn building up to a terrifying and emotional breakdown as the game progresses.

The game is fanciful and beautiful, a graphical piece of art at the time. The gameplay is repetitive from within itself, go here, do this, kill the big daddy, get some more juice and pump yourself up. It's boring and unimaginative.

The storytelling was borrowed from System Shock's progressive method of sharing what happened in audio logs. This is a fantastic way of sharing a story, though the characters that leave the logs need to be believable, true and above all, real to us.

It is not just about fighting, it is about experimenting, adapting, and surviving in a city that wants you dead at every turn. The balance of atmosphere, story, and mechanics is near perfect.

BioShock is not only a game, it is a landmark. A timeless piece of art that changed the medium forever.

Let's compare the game Bioshock to The Simpsons episode titled "Bart Gets Famous," which is the twelfth episode of Season 5.

"Bart Gets Famous" (The Simpsons, Season 5, Episode 12):

**1. Central Theme:

Bioshock: The game delves into themes of objectivism, choice, and the consequences of unchecked power in the underwater city of Rapture.
The Simpsons: "Bart Gets Famous" explores themes of fame, the impact of media and entertainment on society, and the pursuit of success.
**2. Isolation and Unique Setting:

Bioshock: Rapture, an isolated and dystopian underwater city, serves as a unique and atmospheric setting for the game's narrative.
The Simpsons: Bart's moment in the spotlight takes him away from his normal environment, placing him in a unique and unfamiliar setting as he becomes a child star.
**3. Consequences of Pursuing Success:

Bioshock: The player's choices in Bioshock affect the outcome of the story and the fate of Rapture, emphasizing the consequences of pursuing personal objectives without considering the impact on others.
The Simpsons: Bart's pursuit of fame comes with its own set of consequences, showcasing the potential pitfalls and downsides of celebrity culture.
**4. Satirical Elements:

Bioshock: The game incorporates satirical elements, particularly in its critique of Ayn Rand's objectivist philosophy and the dangers of unchecked power.
The Simpsons: "Bart Gets Famous" satirizes the entertainment industry, celebrity culture, and the fleeting nature of fame, providing social commentary with humor.
**5. Exploration of Characters:

Bioshock: The player explores the backgrounds and motivations of characters in Rapture, uncovering the mysteries behind the city and its downfall.
The Simpsons: The episode explores the impact of sudden fame on Bart and the dynamics within the Simpson family, offering insights into the characters' personalities and relationships.
In comparing "Bart Gets Famous" to Bioshock, both explore themes of consequence, the pursuit of personal goals, and the societal impact of individual actions. While the settings and narratives are vastly different, the examination of the human condition and societal issues through humor and storytelling is a common thread in both the episode and the game.

[h1]Intro[/h1]

Before playing this game, I'd heard a lot about it, how people say it's one of them "must-play" & "genre-defining" games. I certainly had my doubts about this, wondering if it was truly all it was made out to be. However, after a play-through, I can full confirm that this game lives up to the hype, and I love it so much!

Note: I did not play the remaster, instead opting to play the original from 2007.

[hr][/hr]

[h1]Gameplay, [b]9.2/10[/b][/h1]

First things first, in my humble opinion, one of the most important parts of a game, is the gameplay, if it's bad, that casts a shadow on the rest of the game. Fortunately, Bioshock has an amazing foundation, between the sweet Plasmid powers you obtain throughout the game, the satisfying guns, and gene tonics. in my almost nine hours of play, there wasn't a moment where I thought combat was getting boring.

This is helped by the fact that the game pretty consistently introduces weapons in its first half, giving you plenty to experiment with. They all have wonderful sound design, and don't feel too weak (unless it's the revolver). Plus the fact that they all have three ammo types helps spice them up, and allow you to judge what's best for the current situation. Every single one feels unique, and like it has its place within the game.

The Plasmids on the other hand, very much serve to let you empower your arsenal, you won't be winning any fights with them alone, but paired with your guns & wrench, you can do some pretty insane things. Don't like all those grenades coming your way? Telekinesis has you covered. Feel like stun-lock is a cool mechanic? Electro Bolt is a nice option for the entire game's cast of enemies. Security cameras giving you too much dang trouble? Security Bullseye has your back, get those flying turrets to fight your enemies! All of these can lead into some really fun combos with your weapons, and I very much encourage experimentation.

When it comes to the smaller buffs, and things you tend to forget about, there's gene tonics, which are both impactful, and not, depending on your mindset when it comes to them. Generally they're pretty set and forget, from what I found, the only time you'll consider changing your current set, is when you get a new one. But even then, I feel most are pretty doo doo, unless they buff your health and/or damage, I usually threw them in cold storage and didn't touch them again.

Now that's all great, how about the enemy variety? Well, I'd say that the game has a pretty diverse selection of enemies, all of them being pretty clearly distinct from one another. Though I will say towards the end of my play-through, it was disappointing to see the same types of enemies over and over. I'd be a little more okay with it if they didn't feel so bullet-spongy at times, but that was more of a minor inconvenience than anything. I feel like they're overall well designed, and play into the other mechanics pretty well, with certain enemies encouraging using different strategies.

The Big Daddies in particular are really fun to fight, and there's plenty of different ways to fight them. Want to set up a web of traps so they instantly die when you bait them into them? Sure thing. Mindlessly spam the electric ammo with the shotgun? Go ahead. Pretend you're a bull rider and get them to ram into walls while you get a few potshots on em? Go for it cowboy. Freeze them in place and sculpt your perfect ice statue? He's your oyster. Or even just stun-lock him until he dies with the chemical thrower? Yeah, it's cheesy, but go ahead.

Onto one of the more, controversial aspects of the game, I guess you could say, the hacking mechanic. Basically just a pipe game where you redirect the water, electricity, whatever it is, into the end point to get er hacked. Some people find this annoying, but I found it to be a fun little break between combat segments, with a pretty decent challenge mid-game. Though I will say that as you progress into the late-game, these puzzles get progressively more frustrating, with you not being able to solve it at all unless you move the first pipe immediately. For some context, each time you fail, you lose some health, so it is quite obnoxious. I'd recommend a stock of auto-hack tools for the late game because of this.

[hr][/hr]

[h1]Visuals, [b]9/10[/b][/h1]

The visuals, oh my my. Coming from the mindset of certain modern gamers, I'd understand if you felt this game is ugly or doesn't look "good enough." But I'd say, more important than the lighting or shadow quality technically, what matters most, is artstyle. If you have a good artstyle, your game will be looking amazing, 10, 20, 30 years down the line. And boy does Bioshock absolutely nail this, to a T.

There aren't many games that make me interested to look around the environment as much as Bioshock, most of the time I just focus on the gameplay because the environments aren't that interesting to look at, and don't tell you much of anything about the in-game world. Of course, Bioshock is different in this regard. I felt like every single nook and cranny had something to look or at or find, and something interesting going on with it.

This especially ties in with the story of the game, where many of the different environments that you'll travel throughtout all have very unique themes, and tell their own story. In terms of gameplay, when you look around, you're rewarded in some pretty big ways, with more loot. Wether that's something as small as some revolver ammo, or as big as a whole new plasmid. All of the environments really go into making Rapture a well thought out and believeable city, with so many things to explore and find out. The lighting of each area is also very well done, and I can really appreciate how beutiful it makes each scene in the game.

There were very few times where I felt like any particular area of the game looked to similar to another, in theme or assets, besides the usual gameplay related aspects, of course. Every level has something different to look at, and that's truly something to appreciate.

[hr][/hr]

[h1]Story, [b]10/10[/b][/h1]

Alright, yeah, I guess there needn't be much preamble for me giving a score like that. I loved Bioshock's story, I loved it a ton. Few games manage to hook me in the first ten minutes and pull me into the narrative, wanting to explore everything I can in the game. From the Little Sisters, Big Daddies, and Splicers, to the titans that control the city of Rapture. In most games, like for instance, Fallout, I'd completely skip over the audio logs and text that tell about the game world, because truly, I don't really care or I'm not interested. With Bioshock however, I found myself traversing environments, eager to find & listen to these voice recordings about all the things going on in Rapture.

The way that everything comes together as the story progresses is amazing, and I feel like as a player, it makes it easy to resonate with who you play as throughout your time, Jack. You also do get to decide, in a pretty big way, how the story goes, but I will have to do another playthrough to see what the alternative route has in store for me. The way that you get to see what has happened in Rapture through the environments you explore is really awesome, truly giving you a perspective on things, rather than them just being told to you by the game.

Anyways, I don't want to delve too deep into the story, because I really think it's something you should go experience for yourself. The many twists and turns it'll take you on are ones I'm sure you'll enjoy. By the end of the game, I actually cried, so if that doesn't convince you it has a good story, I dunno what will, its been the only game capable of accomplishing that feat.

[hr][/hr]

[h1]Overall, [b]9.4/10[/b][/h1]

So to wrap this thing up, I can say with full certainty, that this is one of the best games I've ever played, without a doubt. An absolute ride of gameplay, story, and visuals.

I have played this game multiple times on different consoles, and I have to say - it has withstood the test of time.

Back when I was in 7th grade, i remember watching a schoolmate play this game during a party and was already hooked on the aesthetic and setting, but beyond that - the game is addictive for good reason.

The story is flawed, as many have pointed out, but Bioshock outshines its own shortcomings with relevant commentary, the human condition, and some of the best voice acting in gaming.

I wish we had a third recommend option, because my feelings for this game are honestly mixed and uncertain. It has some pretty strong, good sides, but also some pretty negative sides.

[h2]The Good[/h2]
One of the strongest points this game has is the atmosphere of the environment and story. The setting is unique and interesting, while it guides the player through different areas. It made me want to learn more and wonder what happened to the place.
Having the player being able to choose and level different skills, using different weapons, having limited ammo offers you a good challenge. It also allows you to play in a style that fits how you want to play. It's also fun to experiment and try out new powers and weapon.

[h2]The Bad[/h2]
The enemies and fights. For me, this was where the game became tedious and repetitive. The early part of the game it was all right, but after getting deeper into the game it started feeling like the game was just throwing enemies at you just to throw them at you. It felt like a copy+paste meeting the same enemies over and over. They act the same, behave the same and even look the same. At some parts it didn't feel necessary to meet them at times. It felt like they just threw in some enemies to fill up a blank space to give the player something to do while moving around exploring.
The levels were all right at first, but some of them also felt like a copy+paste. It was like they were doing shortcuts with the levels you can go through. I know they were probably following the theme of the place, but some places were a bit too similar.
The backtracking of this game. It was tedious when you finally have a certain weapon or power, and you can finally get through this certain place or passage, and you had to run all the way back. After a while I just dropped it completely. It didn't feel like it was worth it.

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
I could probably write more but these were my first thoughts when finishing the game. It felt more like a relief to be finished than an achievement. Which means--for me--this game has low replayability. I've heard and read so much praise for this game, but it didn't deliver. It wasn't that bad, and I absolutely love some aspects of it, but it wasn't that amazing either. That's why I'm in the middle about this game. Do I recommend this game? Maybe. Not sure.

[h1]Would You Kindly Play the Remastered Version Instead?[/h1]

[i]BioShock is a shooter unlike any you've ever played, loaded with weapons and tactics never seen. You'll have a complete arsenal at your disposal from simple revolvers to grenade launchers and chemical throwers, but you'll also be forced to genetically modify your DNA to create an even more deadly weapon: you.[/i]

[h2]Story[/h2]
You play as Jack, a silent protagonist aboard a plane over the Atlantic Ocean in 1960. The plane crashes near a mysterious lighthouse in the middle of the ocean. Inside the lighthouse is a bathysphere (a submersible pod) that descends into Rapture, a massive, hidden underwater city. As Jack enters Rapture, he sees it has fallen into chaos. He’s contacted via radio by a man named Atlas, who asks for help rescuing his family and guides Jack through the city.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
BioShock is a first-person shooter, where you explore and fight your way through Rapture. Combat blends traditional gunplay with Plasmid powers, hacking security systems, and setting traps, giving you a wide range of options.

[b][u]Little Sisters & Moral Choices[/u][/b]
Little Sisters can be found in each level, always guarded by a Big Daddy that you have to defeat. Afterwards, you face a choice: rescue for less ADAM and a humane path, or harvest for more ADAM at the cost of her life—a choice that affects your ending.

[b][u]Weapons & Ammo[/u][/b]
You have access to a variety of weapons, including a wrench, revolver, machine gun, shotgun, grenade launcher, chemical thrower, crossbow, and even a camera used to research enemies for damage bonuses. Each weapon can be upgraded twice at Weapon Upgrade Stations. Every weapon has 3 ammo types—like armor-piercing, electric, or explosive rounds. Special ammo can be crafted and rarely found, while common types are available at vending machines or often found.

[b][u]Plasmids & Tonics[/u][/b]
Plasmids are genetic superpowers, almost like spells. EVE is the fuel (like mana) for Plasmids. You can find or buy EVE hypos.

Gene Tonics are passive upgrades and have three classifications: Combat, Physical and Engineering.

Plasmids and Tonics can be found or bought at Gatherer's Garden machines using ADAM. Here you can also buy Plasmid Slots, Gene Tonic Slots, Health Upgrades, and EVE Upgrades. Some Plasmids and Tonics have enhanced versions.

[b][u]Hacking[/u][/b]
Hacking is a core mechanic where you play a pipe-connecting minigame. You can hack security systems like turrets, flying bots, and cameras, but also vending machines, safes, number locks, and health stations. You can also skip hacking with Auto-Hack Tools or buyouts. Hacked bots and turrets will fight for you, cameras will send friendly bots after enemies if they spot any, vending machines have lowered prices, and health stations deal damage to enemies instead.

[h2]Enemies & Bosses[/h2]
[b]Splicers[/b] are the most common enemies in Rapture. Once normal citizens, they've become violent and insane due to Plasmid overuse and ADAM addiction. Splicers come in various types—some focus on melee, others climb walls, teleport and cast fireballs, or use firearms and grenades.

[b]Security systems[/b] are also common enemies and consist of security cameras, bots, gun turrets and rocket turrets.

[b]Big Daddies[/b] are iconic, heavily armored mini-bosses of BioShock. They protect Little Sisters and won't attack you unless provoked.

The enemy AI is good. They react to noise and traps. They will also for example seek water if set on fire and use health stations if injured. Every enemy can be looted when killed.

There are also some unique enemies. These are scripted encounters—more story-driven than regular enemies. There is one boss fight—the final boss.

[h2]Environment[/h2]
The game is set in Rapture, an underwater dystopian city in the 1960s. The game encourages and rewards exploration, as levels are semi-open, with multiple paths and secret areas. The environment is highly interactive. Water can be electrified, and oil puddles can be set on fire to kill enemies. Rapture is filled with security systems that can be hacked and turned to your advantage or used to set traps. Almost everything is lootable—crates, trashcans, cabinets, desks, lockers, cash registers, and more. You can find dollars to spend at vending machines scattered throughout the game.

[h2]Visual Design & Sound Design[/h2]
The world of Rapture is a beautiful yet chaotic underwater city in decay. Many areas are crumbling, with leaking pipes, debris, and fish swimming past shattered windows. Neon signs are frequent, illuminating Rapture in vibrant colors. Big Daddies are hulking figures—flesh and organs fused into armored diving suits, armed with a drill or Rivet Gun. Little Sisters, twisted by ADAM, have yellow eyes and greenish skin, reflecting its cost on the human body, until they’re rescued or harvested. Splicers are grotesquely mutated, often wearing elegant and tattered masquerade outfits and eerie masks.

Big Daddies emit deep, intimidating moans, while Little Sisters speak in eerie, demonic tones that shift to innocent childlike voices when rescued. Splicers often mutter to themselves, revealing their location with unique, unsettling dialogue. Rapture is filled with ambient 1940s-60s music from in-game radios or phonographs, and the constant sound of lapping, dripping, or running water, adding to its haunting atmosphere and reminding you that you’re deep beneath the ocean.

[h2]Constructive Criticism[/h2]
The game crashed several times, resetting my video settings, audio settings, and keybindings each time—sometimes even without crashing, like after I had taken a break and started the game, which was annoying. The settings are also limited, like no brightness option. The mouse sensitivity is absolutely horrible. 

During every cutscene, my character looked down at his feet, obscuring the action; changing resolution didn’t help.

Audio often lagged or bugged out, with missing gunshots and footsteps sounds, forcing me to restart the game frequently.

The hacking mini-game quickly became repetitive and boring, leading me to use auto-hack tools or buyouts instead.

Taking photos of enemies with the camera mid-battle on higher difficulties often leads to your death. An interesting thought, but annoying most of the time.

The story is great, but the ending is very abrupt.

The environment and enemy encounters become somewhat repetitive, with similar corridors, rooms, and foes. There are so many things to loot that you end up looting more than shooting.

[h2]The Verdict[/h2]
The story is memorable and very well-written with some interesting and unpredictable twists, and a truly unique setting and atmosphere. It’s for sure the game’s greatest strength. The combat is fun and offers a range of tactical options through Plasmids, weapons, and hacking systems, though it can start to feel repetitive over time, and the camera mechanic feels impractical on higher difficulties. Technical issues like crashes, audio bugs, and poor settings support noticeably detract from the experience—for that reason alone I recommend you play the remastered version instead. Obey.

So, you know, it escalated quickly. Let’s talk about the intro. You crash into the ocean, swim to a mysterious lighthouse, take a bathysphere ride down into the sea, and BAM—Rapture. An underwater city full of philosophical graffiti, broken dreams, and vending machines that scream at you. It’s stunning. It’s terrifying. It’s also completely abandoned except for the homicidal maniacs and giant men in vintage diving suits stomping around with power drills. Vacation destination of the year. The combat? A chaotic ballet of guns, fire hands, and “oh no I accidentally electrocuted myself again.” Plasmids let you do everything from shooting bees out of your arms to mind-controlling enemies, which raises questions that science should never answer. And the Big Daddies? They’re like boss fights combined with emotional damage. You want to fight them. You also kind of want to hug them. (You shouldn't.) But let’s be honest: you're here for the story. The atmosphere. The vibes. This game doesn’t just pull the rug out from under you—it tears out the floorboards, drops you into a moral philosophy class, and then politely hands you a wrench. And just when you think you’re getting the hang of it—BOOM. Plot twist so good it made me question if I was being mind-controlled by my microwave the whole time. Also, shoutout to the audio diaries. There Are many things good with the original Bioshock game, but there a few gripes I have with the game. During the main story there are a few glitches and bugs (I was playing the non-remastered edition) but nothing major, mostly just rare occasional crashes, too intense for the physics engine to handle (same with the 2nd game, but more on that over there).
The introduction of the plasmids and weapons were very fluid and intuitive and at the ADAM stations, the prices for ammo, plasmids, and tonics were very balanced the entire course of the game. The Game is also very well put together story-wise, aside from at the ending of the game. In which (at least the good ending, I haven't played the other ending) seems very forced onto the player, you get a happy ever after with all the Little Sisters, and not more of a realistic ending where it works out, but some things don't. 

One good thing in the game are the Plasmids; they are the genetic encoding power-ups you get throughout your journey in Rapture. Some are unlocked through Story progression, meanwhile others are rewards for harvesting ADAM, or even just exploring the different rooms in the game, although most are just bought at the ADAM vending machine. They are pretty balanced, being you as the player needs to be able to use plasmids, as well as using the Weapons in order to fairly get through the game. They need to work together, not seperate power systems throughout the game. for example you can get the frost blast plasmid and then freeze a big daddy stunning him. Then you can shoot him with other weapons while he is frozen, which they balance with the incinerate ability (fire blast). which if you use ice and then fire, it just melts the ice, not being able to have both active on an enemy. Another Good aspect of the game is the Weapons; during my play-through I mostly used the Shotgun, Wrench, and Tommy Gun. Throughout the game you can upgrade your weapons, but only up to 7~ times throughout the game collectively, across all your weapons, so you must choose wisely. Even on easy mode, you will want those upgrades. 

Another positive element about the Original Bioshock is the story. You are the sole survivor (or so you think) of a plane crash and stumble upon a lighthouse, bringing you to the great underwater city of RAPTURE. Here, you find your first plasmid on the surface, and are communicating with someone known as Atlas; in which he asks you to help him with helping out in recovering someone/something he needs from the city. "Would you kindly?". Where it leads to you going around a relatively small portion of rapture, searching, finding out what ADAM is, seeing the remaining residents of the broken city; and most of all Andrew Ryan, the supposed crooked villain of the story. But all is revealed throughout the story, As you collect ADAM and grow stronger. In order to escape you will have to turn into a Big Daddy, in order to both, lure the Little Sisters to help you (in the good ending), and it adds an extra layer of defence, armour, and protection to you for the Final Boss fight. Although this is a good game, there are some plot-holes that arise and are never acknowledged in the subsequent games being Bioshock 2 and Infinite. 

All in all, Bioshock 1 is a pretty solid game, story and game-play-wise, but overall does lack just that extra oomph that is to be desired.

BioShock is considered an FPS classic, bringing in mechanics and ideas that is today considered typical for most games in that genre. Does it hold up? Both yes and no.

The story in Bioshock is mainly told through pre-recorded tapes and radio communications with other characters. At the time it was an interesting way to convey the story in a game that was mostly action, but as more games starting taking after it got old pretty quick. But the world building is still intriguing, you have Rapture which is underground city built by a business man who essentially goes full Ayn Rand, wantingto build his own libertarian society without kings, governments and religion - only man. When you arrive to Rapture however, all of those dreams are crushed. Instead you arrive to the aftermath of an event that occurred on New Years Eve 1959.

It is noticable that the devs of Bioshock wanted you to be able to do a lot within the game, following the pattern of its predecessor System Shock. You have various weaponry together with the powers you can acquire through using injectable plasmids (telekinesis, fire and electric powers, etc.). But in the end it feels too much, as there is also a hacking and crafting system thrown in which makes you as the player having to keep up with a lot of different gameplay mechanics and systems.

Overall, it is not a bad game by any means but playing it today you realize that both the genre and the way the game wants to do its story telling has progressed beyond it. It is a game that really paved the way though, and for that it should be given the recognisition it deserves. Unfortunately it is one of those games that you probably just play once or twice, and then never again.

[h2] Style Over Substance [/h2] 

The more times I go back to Bioshock, the more glaring a lot of its faults become to me. 

I'll always appreciate how the game accurately depicts the logical conclusion of an anarcho-capitalistic society, the game gets really full of its own philosophy and intellectual enlightenment yet rarely conveys it into a compelling story or in moment to moment gameplay. 

It does the Half-Life approach of giving you the illusion that you're in charge of your own destiny, while the game design and the NPCs in your head basically guide you on a rail from start to finish, with morality choices and character decisions barely mattering and the game going from fascinating set pieces to basically busywork of deactivating alarms, puzzle minigames and dealing with an ever-increasing number of bullet sponge enemies. 

But we rarely remember this game's faults, shortcomings and questionable decisions. Because none of that really matters when you get lost in the decaying, destroyed remnants of Rapture. It's twisted, it's dark, it's bleak and it's absolutely beautiful. Helps that the game for the most part swaps the scatological yellow and brown of the 7th gen for bluer hues that make the grime and blood and wreckage much more palatable, and the crumbling art deco aesthetic is just so well done. 

It was style over substance back in the day and is even more so now with the power of hindsight and reflection, but man is that style just kind of immaculate. 

Game goes for pretty cheap on sale. Worth it for the atmosphere, but if you come out of the game thinking Ayn Rand had a point or something along those lines, please read a book. Any book will do.

Ah, [u]BioShock[/u]. This 2007 cult classic is more than just a first-person shooter, it’s an immersive and unforgettable experience that has made video game history. Developed by Irrational Games and led by visionary Ken Levine, BioShock plunges us into the underwater city of Rapture, a dystopian utopia where the ideals of a free world without constraints have turned into a nightmare. Is it a timeless classic or an aging game that rests a little too much on its laurels? Let’s explore the depths of this masterpiece together and discover what really lies in the dark corners of Rapture.

[b]Good points[/b]
[u]Captivating and deep storyline:[/u] Heart of BioShock is its story. Inspired by the philosophy of Ayn Rand and the ideals of radical capitalism, the narrative explores the extreme consequences of a society where individualism and total freedom are pushed to their limits. The once beautiful and prosperous city of Rapture lies in ruins, consumed by greed, madness, and power struggles. Every street corner, every audio recording found, and every encounter with Rapture's strange characters adds layers of depth and mystery. You quickly find yourself drawn into this descent into hell, asking yourself existential and philosophical questions while fighting for your survival.

[u]Unique and oppressive atmosphere:[/u] From the moment you descend into the elevator to Rapture, you feel a palpable tension. The flashing lights, the eerie shadows, the whispering voices of the Splicers... BioShock excels at creating a breathtaking atmosphere. The soundtrack is a mix of eerie orchestras and 50s tunes, adding a retro touch and a constant sense of unease. The graphics, while a little dated today, still contribute to the creepy and claustrophobic atmosphere of Rapture. The developers have masterfully used lighting, art deco decoration and sound effects to immerse you in this immersive universe.

[u]Big Daddies and the Little Sisters:[/u] Big Daddies, these immense protectors in rusty spacesuits, are the emblem of BioShock. These encounters are often moments of pure terror and excitement. Armed with your courage and your Plasmids, each fight against a Big Daddy is a challenge, where strategy and survival mix. Then comes the moral decision: what to do with the Little Sister he was protecting? The mechanic of choosing between "save" or "harvest" adds an emotional and ethical dimension that marks the players.

[u]Plasmids and the variety of gameplay:[/u] Plasmids are genetic modifications that grant you supernatural powers: electrocuting your enemies, throwing fireballs, or summoning swarms of insects. This mechanic introduces diversity to the gameplay, allowing players to customize their playstyle. BioShock encourages you to experiment and combine these powers with traditional weapons, making each fight unique and dynamic.

[b]Bad points[/b]
[u]Gameplay that can get repetitive:[/u] Despite the variety of Plasmids and weapons, BioShock sometimes suffers from a certain redundancy. Encounters can become mechanical, especially in the second half of the game where enemy types are more or less the same and new powers are few and far between. Some players may tire of the "explore-combat-collect items" pattern that structures the gameplay.

[u]Choice mechanics that lack depth:[/u] While BioShock boasts of having important moral choices, these choices are actually quite limited and do not have as deep an impact as one might hope. The choice to save or harvest the Little Sisters is interesting, but it doesn't fundamentally affect the flow of the game, aside from the two different endings. This lack of real impact of the choices can disappoint players looking for depth in the consequences of their decisions.

[u]Sometimes flawed AI:[/u] Enemy AI is not always up to par. Splicers can be unpredictable, but often in a bad way. It is not uncommon to see enemies get stuck in scenery or act inconsistently, spoiling the immersion and tension of the fights a little.

[u]Some aging aspects:[/u] Although BioShock's graphics have aged well overall, some technical aspects are now dated. Animations can sometimes seem stiff, and textures sometimes lack finesse, especially when compared to more recent games. Thankfully, a remastered version has improved some of these elements, but it's still worth noting for modern gamers.

[b]Summary[/b]
[u]BioShock[/u] is a masterpiece for good reason. Its rich narrative, unique atmosphere, and ability to question the player on philosophical topics set it apart from most classic shooters. While it has some gameplay weaknesses and some technical aspects have aged, the experience remains captivating and memorable. Playing BioShock is diving into a reflection on society, power, and the limits of utopia. If you've never explored Rapture, it's time to take your courage in both hands and descend into the depths. Because once you're down, as Andrew Ryan so aptly puts it, you end up asking yourself only one question: Does a man have the right to choose?

2) Lack of enemy variety. When I originally played a disc version of this game 12 years ago, I was complaining that it was mainly "splicers" (human mutants with either melee attacks or ranged attacks such as guns or explosives) and my friend basically said "Nah man it aint that bad. There's some enemy variety" but I had left the game halfway through and didn't finish it until I tried it again when I bought it on Steam on sale. But really it's just some boring human enemies and occasionally you fight big daddies which are the drill guys you see on this game's cover art along with another big guy with a gun called "Rosies". The Rosies are really annoying because they're bullet sponges with sniper tier weapons. Idk how you're supposed to dodge them other than peeking a bunch and trying to get them to melee you instead. I guess you could say the auto-turrents you fight are enemies too especially since there's some robot enemies but that'd at best be three enemy categories. 

Let's go with Half-Life 2 for comparison. You had combine dudes and their variants (metrocops and combine dudes with various weapons), zombies (three distinct types that have to be approached differently, four if you count the zombine from the episodes), antlions, turrents, "vehicles" (striders, helicopters, etc.), and also a large variety of hazards (Bioshock has ONE type of hazard). We could also include headcrabs as their own category but I think I've made my point clear. There's at least 5 truly distinct enemies and they even had special areas where there's a large presence of them like with Ravenholm and Nova Prospekt. 

Bioshock on the other hand is 80% splicers and 20% everything else.

3) The story is not "genius" or anything. I'll just leave it at that. It would be cool if the user had an actual choice but there's only one thing, a pretty important thing I might add, but still only one aspect you control and that's whether you want to kill little girls or save them.

You can swap upgrades at any time.  This game is called a "Spiritual Successor to System Shock" but the only things those two have in common is magic powers, hacking minigames (which Bioshock does a poor job compared to System Shock 1 especially), and having the word "shock" in the name. 

5) Hacking sucks. It gets repetitive and difficulty is more so from really bad starting positions and not clicking to "uncover" tiles fast enough. Make sure to get an upgrade that slows the flow speed because those first moves are make or break since it can lead you to a dead end. Use an auto-clicker to uncover tiles faster and so your finger doesn't hurt.

6) No subtitles... but you can read what the characters said AFTER they said it to you by going into your journal.

7) No proper inventory system and also arbitrary carry limits. You can carry like 400 smg bullets but only 200 armor piercing smg bullets. You can carry 12 grenades but only 6 proximity mines. Why? Why is it set up like this? Buzz off. There's even a limit to how much money you can carry. You can only carry $500 even though the indicator shows 4 digits. BioShock, released in 2007 by 2K Games and developed by Irrational Games, is one of the most iconic and influential FPS games of all time. Combining deep storytelling, immersive world-building, and unique gameplay mechanics, BioShock delivers an unforgettable experience that blends philosophical themes with tense survival horror elements.

Whether you're exploring the haunting underwater city of Rapture for the first time or replaying to catch every detail, BioShock remains an absolute must-play.

Why BioShock is a Timeless Classic
🌊 Incredible Setting – Welcome to Rapture
The game’s biggest strength is Rapture, a beautifully crafted underwater dystopia, built as a utopia of freedom and innovation but ultimately destroyed by greed, power, and madness. From the moment you descend into the ocean, the game grips you with its haunting atmosphere and stunning Art Deco architecture.

📖 A Deep and Thought-Provoking Story
BioShock is more than just an FPS—it’s a narrative masterpiece. It explores themes of free will, objectivism, and morality, heavily inspired by Ayn Rand’s philosophy. The story twists and turns in unexpected ways, leading to one of the most famous plot twists in gaming history.

🔫 Satisfying and Unique Gameplay
The mix of guns and Plasmids (genetic powers) creates incredibly fun combat. You can freeze enemies, set them on fire, electrocute water puddles, or turn enemies against each other. This freedom allows for creative and strategic encounters.

🧬 Little Sisters and Big Daddies – A Moral Dilemma
Throughout the game, you must decide whether to harvest or save the Little Sisters, which affects the story’s outcome. Protecting or fighting the terrifying Big Daddies, their monstrous guardians, makes for some of the most intense fights in the game.

🎶 Incredible Sound Design and Atmosphere
The eerie 50s-era music, distant whale calls, and creepy echoes of insane Splicers roaming Rapture make every corridor unsettling. The voice acting is also top-tier, with unforgettable performances that bring Rapture’s tragic inhabitants to life.

Any Flaws?
❌ Some Clunky Combat Mechanics
The shooting mechanics can feel a little stiff compared to modern FPS games, but the unique powers and strategy compensate for this.

❌ Hacking Minigame Can Be Repetitive
Hacking turrets and vending machines is useful, but the pipe-connecting minigame gets old fast. Fortunately, later games refined this mechanic.

Conclusion
BioShock isn’t just a great game—it’s a work of art. Its story, setting, and atmosphere make it a must-play for any gamer who loves deep narratives and immersive worlds.

Released roughly 10 years after System Shock 2, Bioshock (the 'shock' in the title is on purpose) is the spiritual successor to SS2. Beginning life as another sci-fi horror game set aboard a station, the game would eventually shift themes to an underground Nazi laboratory before settling on the Art Deco underwater motif. Which is quite a trip. From SS2's deep-space to the bottom of the ocean, this started as SS3 before settling on being a 'spiritual successor' with a new world altogether.

	Bioshock takes place in Rapture, an underwater, man-made city. It's guiding philosophy is best exemplified by a prominent banner the player sees at the very start: “No Gods or Kings. Only Man.' (a fantastically evocative phrase). In other words, Rapture is a Laissez-faire society, where the artist, scientist, doctor, and entrepreneur is free from 'parasites' that would otherwise stifle progress. And who are the 'parasites'? Big government taxation; Communist collectivists, and the poor seeking wealth redistribution. Churches with their moral objections to research. Environmentalists. Etc.

	Bioshock's world is therefore Ayn Rand brought to life. Err...game. Brought to game. If you're really interested, look into Objectivism-her philosophical work. Bioshock is a Capitalist utopia that is facing some unsavory consequences in its minimal regulation. The poor are taken advantage of and used as stock, with orphans in particular being 'put to work'. Morality would reasonably get in the way of progress at times (think the Nazi experiments on humans). In a society that is unchained from that morality, you have social strife and civil turmoil. As well as extreme wealth and advancements.

	One of  those achievements is the discovery of ADAM, which is a material that allows for the genetic modification of humans. It's the perfect plot device for a society obsessed with progress with no moral limitation: an amazing achievement in genetics, with human suffering as a side effect. ADAM allows the ugly to become beautiful, as well as telekinetic abilities. Like electric shock, levitation of items, etc. In a competitive society suffering from emerging social strife, it plays into the hands of militias, corporate warfare, and the everyday minutae of keeping up with the competition. Everyone eventually becomes 'addicted' to this material, losing their sanity without regular injections of it.

	If this sounds like I'm spoiling the story, I'm really not. It's all told within the first level. There's a more personal story at play here, with the protagonist's entry into Rapture (unwilling entry, that is). He's thrust into the current civil war and destruction, assisting a character in finding his wife and child. I won't spoil a lot there, but I will note that the game has a very ingenious 'twist' at play. And the main character is much more closely related to the happenings in the underwater city than originally thought.

	ADAM is not just a narrative element, it's also a game feature. An interesting one, because to me it represents what Psionics in SS2 tried to be. ADAM is much better than Psionics. And it's mostly because it separates the passive abilities from the 'active' ones that are used in battle. Plasmids allow you combat abilities that interact with the environment, whilst Gene Tonics provide passive benefits. Reminder that in SS2 both required activation and only remained for a set period of time. And the combat abilities were few and rather uncreative. Whereas in Bioshock you can set up traps.

	If Plasmids are Psionics done right, everything else is merely carried over from SS2 with minor enhancements. Ammo types are present once more. Security cameras and turrets. Even hacking. Only the hacking mini-game is more than just RNG. You solve a puzzle whereby you divert a liquid to its proper end-point. Everything from SS2 carries over, only it's done better or more competently.

	About the only thing I'd argue this game 'lacks' over SS2 is map complexity. SS's map had you backtrack to previous areas. Frequently. They all felt like part of a larger whole, as opposed to levels that exist separately from one another. While you can traverse back to previous levels in Bioshock, you will never have to backtrack between levels to progress. And while there are multiple rooms that require exploration within levels, you'll never get lost. It's simpler.

	Which isn't to say the level design is bad, but it's a point worth bringing up in the comparison. And since we're on the topic of levels, I should mention how incredible the art is for this game. The levels aren't just corridors. They're art pieces. Seriously.

	In fact, Bioshock was displayed at Smithsonian American Art Museum in Washington, D.C (in 2012). In a 'Video Games as Art' exhibit. The game is littered with ads, musical pieces, and glimpses of the ocean surrounding the undersea metropolis. It's wonderfully creative, and evocative of 1920's America. 

	The 'video games as art' argument doesn't just rest on the visual, either. Bioshock is an incredibly unique game in it's themes. Obviously the philosophy of Objectivism wasn't coined by the Bioshock writers, but it's certainly not a common theme in games or any other media of the time. And the implications of such a worldview are brought out in interesting manners in the game world. I recall all the conversations about the underlying philosophy and how it did, or could have, played out in the game world. And it's rare for games to inspire such spirited and substantive debate.

	But even beyond the 'world lore', there is a well thought out and captivating drama taking place in the background. Of a protagonist living a lie and unknowingly being taken advantage of. Which plays into the larger 'Man as the creator of his own destiny' philosophy, which is ingenious. 

	The only real, objective issue with the game is that it is (supposedly) difficult to launch. Bioshock runs on a heavily modified version of Unreal Engine 2, which is probably why so many people experience technical issues with it. I didn't, but I see all the guides and forum threads asking and offering solutions. And yes, this game looks incredible even today (probably due to good art direction), but it's actually running on an extremely outdated game engine (even for the time). 

	There is a 'remaster' whose purpose is entirely to get the game to run on modern systems. Because it doesn't 'remaster' anything. If anything, it actually looks worse in certain parts. But whatever the case, and however you play the game, it's one of those 'hall of fame' type of games that everyone should play. My praise for SS2 carries over to Bioshock. Only in much stronger terms.

[h1] Reviewed for Steam Deck [/h1]
[h3] Stability: 7/10 [/h3]
This game is listed as [b] Playable [/b] and I agree although I ran into a few issues. The game crashed to desktop a few times during my playthrough. I also left the game idling on the pause screen and came back to find the audio "sped up" (so "Save and Exit" if you intend to be AFK for a while). Other than these, I encountered no other bugs during my playtime.
[h3] Gameplay: 9/10 [/h3]
This game features combat using a range of weapons and powers. In addition, each weapon has different ammunition and each power has different levels to it. This leads to a large variety of combinations the player can use during their playthrough. For instance, you can run-and-gun your way through using a machine gun and flame powers or you can be tactical by charming your foes and laying traps. There are many different enemies, some requiring different methods to efficiently defeat and keeping the player on their toes. 
[h3] Playtime/Replayability:  8/10 [/h3]
The playtime of this game short to moderate (depending on the player it can be 8 hours or longer). Fully exploring the maps may add a few more hours of gameplay (ie: trying to find all the voice logs). The storyline is linear, so you can experience it all in one playthrough (excluding the voice logs). However, given the variety of gameplay styles, I can see this being replayed every so often.
[h3] Story/World: 8/10 [/h3]
If you aren't paying attention or collecting voice logs, the story of BioShock can be missed. Even if you are paying attention, it can be confusing at times. However, delving into the lore of Rapture and its inhabitants reveals an interesting plot full of social/political/economic themes and debate of freedom vs. order (as well as morality vs. power). The ending, albeit abrupt, is a great twist that was unexpected on my first playthrough. The world is novel, mixing 40s art style with futuristic technology in an underwater setting (not unlike "Fallout" but it seems to distance itself in a good way).  The enemies are menacing and eerie, fitting well into the post-apocalyptic setting. 
[h3] Audio/Visual 7/10 [/h3]
This game is quite dated, so don't expect stunning graphics. That being said, it ran at a stable 60 fps and I didn't encounter any graphical glitches in my playthrough. The sound design still holds up though. The various enemies (especially Big Daddies) inspire terror by just hearing them in the room. The voice acting from the main characters Andrew Ryan and Atlas are great. The soundtrack hits a mix or retro tunes to hold the setting and a theatrical score. Both are great and I recommend a listen even if you don't play the game. 
[h3] Overall: 8/10 [/h3]
Even after all this time, this game still scratches an itch for horror-action gameplay. The gameplay, story, setting, and sound merit at least one playthrough (if not more). It's frequently on sale, so pick it up when you can. It's a valuable addition to anyone who enjoys a good story and a good scare.

The first part of the BioShock series of games was born. The game developers squeezed all the juices out of the Unreal Engine, which was popular at that time, and the visual part of the game turned out to be simply amazing! The visualization of water deserves special attention. The game will be a pleasure to play even in our time. I personally completed the game about a month ago and got an unforgettable pleasure from passing it.


Noting the graphic component, I also want to highlight the plot of the game. The main character, who survived the plane crash, finds himself in an underwater town called Rapture and, guided by tips from a certain person named Atlas, plows the underwater expanses. For the first few minutes, the game seemed a little boring to me. The plot was completely incomprehensible, but towards the end of the game a lot became clear, I will not disclose the details - you need to feel it yourself during the passage. In addition, there are several endings of the game. In general, the plot turned out to be full of unexpected twists and exciting moments.

The gameplay cannot be called diverse, but the language cannot be called monotonous either. The combat system is decorated with the presence of plasmids - gene modifications that give the hero Superpowers. As the game progresses, you will find more and more new plasmids. They are bought for ADAM, which you will receive by saving or emptying little sisters. I advise you to save them, it will have a positive effect on the end of the game. I really regretted emptying a couple of sisters at the beginning of the game and ended up watching the worst possible ending.

There are quite a lot of weapons in the game, but they also appear during the game. At the end, you will already have about 8 different types of weapons in your arsenal: from a revolver to a grenade launcher and a crossbow. Killing mutants becomes a pleasure. Combinations of plasmids and weapons make each fight colorful and spectacular. You won't see this in any other game.

[h3]Would you kindly stop scrolling and read this review[/h3]

Bioshock was groundbreaking in the way it introduced many gamers to an obscure art style and a niché political philosophy; namely art deco and objectivism. Both of these are weaved into the games DNA and helped to create its iconic look, deeply immersive and memorable world, and its well written story and characters.

The opening few minutes are also iconic and almost perfect in the way they introduce the player to these two concepts, as well as to one of the game's antagonists, Andrew Ryan. It is mostly on the rails and involves lots of delightful visual storytelling as well as a recorded speech from Ryan. As the haunting music sores your 'ride' culminates in a sudden reveal of Bioshock's underwater city, Rapture, a place founded by Ryan in the hopes it would become an objectivist utopia.

"[I]I am Andrew Ryan, and I'm here to ask you a question. Is a man not entitled to the sweat of his brow? 'No!' says the man in Washington, 'It belongs to the poor.' 'No!' says the man in the Vatican, 'It belongs to God.' 'No!' says the man in Moscow, 'It belongs to everyone.' I rejected those answers; instead, I chose something different. I chose the impossible. I chose... Rapture[/I]"

On arriving in the city it quickly becomes clear that Rapture is far from a utopia and that something has gone very, very wrong. 

Now I'm no political expert, but it's obvious from Andrew Ryan's opening monologue that this is a world built on objectivism. As I understand it, objectivism, a philosophy cooked up by Ayn Rand, is a form of right wing, hyper libertarianism, married to extreme capitalism. If selfish greed were a political philosophy, it would be objectivism. The needs of the few outweigh the needs of the many, as a mirror universe version of Spock might say.

Bioshock isn't a celebration of Rand's politics though; as you explore Rapture you'll quickly realise through the narrative that this is a critique of Ayn Rand's political philosophy. It turns out that in an underwater city where everyone is working for themselves, nothing useful or necessary gets done and there's no-one to do the menial, less 'creative and fulfilling' jobs; those jobs that are vital to maintaining and running a vast underwater city. There is also no money to pay the people who are needed to do those jobs, and no supervision.

The citizens of Rapture also discovered a substance called Adam. When refined into a Plasmid, Adam rewrites a person's genetic material, giving them superhuman abilities. One of the downsides of plasmids use is their addictive qualities and they can also cause mental and physical degradation when over used. The second 'person' you see in Rapture is a victim of Adam abuse and has lost their mind, becoming a murder happy Splicer. You see them through a small window, gutting the first person you see. So Plasmid use isn't healthy; luckily as the player you will inject yourself with many many plasmids!

In a democratic society, regulation, ethical considerations and/or law enforcement of some kind could have led to better safeguards and more thorough testing of Adam. But in Rapture that would be hampering creative genius.

Then some sort of conflict began on new years eve 1958, between factions loyal to Ryan and those loyal to somebody named Atlas. With plasmids added to the mix things clearly didn't go so well, and this becomes apparent soon after you 'land'. Things are fucked, to put it mildly.

You piece a lot of this together within the first hour or so through the visuals alone. Rapture's beautiful, clean, simple, symmetrical 1920's art deco face is cracking. The imposing bronze sculptures are tarnished and some are toppled; the gold plaques are grimy, and the green marble and ceramic tiles are pitted, shattered and broken. There are leaks everywhere too; maintenance having been largely abandoned. The city is flooding and large parts of it are without power. Machinery is malfunctioning and there are there are bodies all over the place. Many of the dead are in evening wear that is age worn and tattered. Some are wearing masks, like they died during a masked ball. The Splicers are similarly attired but those without masks are horrifyingly deformed. Mutated.

The atmosphere is unsettling and meloncholic, and sometimes, when the lights are flickering, casting strange shadows and the faint, nonsensical noises of one of Rapture's mad citizens are getting ever louder, and closer, the game is outright frightening.

This would be a decent way to tell a story but there are also audiologs made by the citizens before things went to shit, and NPCs that aren't currently trying to kill you. When taken together this is world building at its finest. Later on you'll start learning about the player character and their connection to Rapture, the two philosophies of Ryan and Atlas and the ultimate fate of the city. This is the game's story and it's wonderfully paced and told, and  incredibly immersive.

I'd be remiss if I didn't talk about the gameplay, but it's only important as a part of the whole, nothing about the FPS mechanics is outstanding. None of the guns are particularly memorable but they sound meaty enough and can be upgraded, as well as fitted out with different ammo types. You can also hack cameras and sentry bots to help you in combat, and these skills, along with heath and energy can be levelled up. You need the energy to use plasmids. There are a large number of plasmids, some of which you find and others you have to buy. They too can be levelled up and range from basic magical attacks like incinerate, winter blast and electrobolt, which are pretty self explanatory, to more tactical ones such as telekinesis, a decoy and one that charms enemies to fight for you. 

Enemy variety is a rather limited, there are only a few different types of Splicer, but each benefits from a slightly different approach to takedown, and there are generally plasmids that are better at countering certain Splicers. Encounters can be hectic if there are multiple Splicer types and then there are the big baddies. Not Splicers themselves, these armoured giants stomp around Rapture often in the footsteps of small girls. These little sisters are Adam gatherers* and you need Adam to buy plasmids, but before you can deal with the little sisters you have to get rid of daddy. Now you can just leave these pairings be when you encounter them, and as long as you don't get too close to the child the big daddy won't attack. It's always worth it though, and these fights can be some of the best, and worst when they're messy, in the game, requiring lots of ammo and plasmid use. 

This is where the game's morality system comes into play, you can 'harvest' the little sisters for a large amount of Adam, killing them, or release them from their drugged servitude, saving them for little material gain. It's one of those shit good/evil binary choices that video games do, that are never really choices because the good option is obviously the one to go, especially if it effects the ending. You're not even really punished for choosing the good option because after you've saved enough little sisters they'll drop off presents stuffed with Adam. It's definitely one of the most poorly thought out aspects of BioShock, along with the hacking mini game. Nothings perfect though. 

I've wasted enough of your time. Bioshock is a fantastic game worthy of its iconic status; it's beautiful, dark, deep,, smart, engrossing and unforgettable. Get it.

BioShock is a first-person shooter game that explores the themes of free will, morality, and power in a dystopian underwater city called Rapture. While not set in the same universe, BioShock is often seen as a spiritual successor to the seminal System Shock games.

You crash land on (on top of) the city of Rapture, and as you descend, you journey through a world which has seemingly gone to hell in a handbasket - and quickly. Featuring (quite possibly) the most amazing water effects in any game ever, your mission is to make your way through the city, figure out what has happened, and ultimately attempt to escape. Key to this are the entities referred to as "little sisters" and the currency ADAM - this is your gateway to plasmids and tonics, which end up providing a lite RPG element to the game as you have limited slots available to you. Herein lies the premise of the world and its choices (whether real or imagined): how much power do you want? How much are you willing to fight to get more ADAM (you must deal with the guardians in order to interact with a little sister - no small task on higher difficulties)? How will you respond once in that position? While you could in theory play much of the game without gathering more ADAM, you will neuter the experience for yourself by doing so. While the ultimate outcome of your choices may not make all that much difference, perhaps the real winner here (and appeal for those more intellectually/existentially inclined) is the question of how things evolve/devolve in the absence of any restriction, i.e. "free will" as Andrew Ryan preaches.

There are not many points in the game to critique: enemies can be real bullet sponges (especially on higher difficulties), the Circus of Values jingle is incredibly annoying with the tone and how often you hear it, balance in the early game feels off (you are properly underpowered until you get going), and the spawning system occasionally borders on ludicrous. Many times, I had cleared a room with only one entry point, only to have an enemy suddenly appear in the room or even the same room as me. It is not a big issue, but it is jarring enough to break the immersion ([spoiler]perhaps feasible for Houdini splicers, but otherwise no[/spoiler]).

I may have been fortunate in the sense of not having any issues getting it to run (although I did introduce some problems attempting to use the tweaker, ending with the game refusing to launch until I went back to normal). If you are one of the unfortunates - you may find many useful tips at the PCGamingWiki page (https://www.pcgamingwiki.com/wiki/BioShock). For more specific issues to the Steam version, the below may be useful (all credit to OP):
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=266981933
In terms of comparison to the remaster - there may not be a compelling reason to choose one over the other. The remastered version comes with higher resolution textures, higher resolutions supported natively, FOV slider in game (VERY important), and overall ran much smoother for me. The original version also does not have the Challenge Rooms included, nor does ALT-TAB work properly unless you quit to the main menu first. These points may however be moot, as buying the one gives you the other anyway. Again, I may have been fortunate in not having major issues running either one.

Whichever path you end up choosing - BioShock deserves to be played; it is a fine example of immersive storytelling and atmospheric setting. Now, would you kindly click that button and enjoy the game?

When BioShock first surfaced in 2007, it wasn't just another first-person shooter — it was a seismic shift in how narrative and gameplay could intertwine. A bold blend of dystopian storytelling, atmospheric world-building, and moral complexity, BioShock raised the bar for what games could be. Nearly two decades later, its legacy remains intact, even if some of its mechanics show their age.

An unforgettable setting. The underwater city of Rapture is the crown jewel of BioShock. Dripping with Art Deco decadence, rusted machinery, and eerie silence, Rapture feels like a living character — beautiful, broken, and full of secrets. Every corner tells a story. Every audio diary, sign, or shattered storefront adds to the slow unraveling of a society that once believed it could escape the constraints of morality, government, and god.

A story with real weight. BioShock doesn’t just ask players to shoot their way through enemies; it challenges them to think. Through the philosophy of Andrew Ryan, the tragedy of genetic excess, and the unforgettable mid-game twist (you know the one), it deconstructs the illusion of player agency in clever, meta-textual ways. The “Would you kindly…” moment remains one of the most powerful narrative gut punches in video game history.

Gameplay with flexibility. The combination of conventional firearms and plasmid powers allows for creative combat. You can set traps, freeze enemies, ignite oil slicks, or hack security drones to fight for you. It’s not a run-and-gun shooter — it’s a sandbox of cause and effect, and the game often rewards experimentation.

Moral choices that matter. The Little Sisters — genetically altered children who harvest a substance called ADAM — present one of the game's central ethical dilemmas: do you save them and gain less ADAM, or harvest them for personal gain? The mechanic is simple, but it adds real tension and feeds into the game’s themes of control, consequence, and free will.

Combat can feel clunky. While the variety is impressive, weapon feedback and enemy AI don’t always hold up to modern standards. Hit detection is occasionally wonky, and some enemy types can become repetitive by the game’s latter half.

The final act stumbles a bit. After the story’s mid-point crescendo, the last hour or two feels more traditional and less inspired, culminating in a final boss that lacks the nuance of the narrative that precedes it.

Visual aging. While the art direction remains top-tier, the original textures and animations (in the non-remastered version) show their age. That said, Rapture’s design still shines through thanks to exceptional style over sheer fidelity.

BioShock isn’t just a game — it’s a philosophical experience wrapped in a shooter’s clothing. Its questions about freedom, power, and the illusion of choice linger long after the credits roll. Though some mechanics may feel dated today, the core of BioShock — its ambition, storytelling, and atmosphere — is timeless.

If you’ve never explored the depths of Rapture, now’s the time. And if you have, there’s always something new to discover on a return trip.

what makes bioshock so special?

is it the setting? the 50s art deco meets nuclear shelteresque underwater vibes is definitely one of the most iconic settings in gaming, helped by noirish graphics such as great water effects as you walk under a waterfall and your vision gets distorted and dramatic shadows foreshadowing your upcoming enemies. but as bioshock infinite arguably shows, you can waste away a good setting with a poor story and gameplay

is it the story then? the plot twist is one of the most iconic in gaming. the theme of a lack of choices is subtly built up in the beginning (you only have limited slots for your plasmids/tonics and you have to choose which ones to equip and which ones to stash? how curious!). it’s ironic how a game hailing from a heritage of ‘choice-focused’ immersive sims is now telling the world that actually, video game choices are not yours to invent. but the plot doesn’t really make sense; you are essentially shuttled from random location to random location. and the game really starts to unravel its own logic after the plot twist (tenenbaum easily removed the would you kindly-phrase from your brain)

is it the gameplay? you’re given ample tools to play around with which are super fun, especially the plasmids. levels are fun to traverse, balancing nicely between sprawling yet clear to traverse and know what the objective is. which is the motto of the game mechanics; they look intimidatingly complex but they’re actually approachable. however, imsim purists have decried this game for not giving you total emergent gameplay freedom, and they’re right; yeah you can pit turrets against big daddies but c’mon, you’re emptying your shotgun and grenade launchers when you see them. also, the weapons are janky as hell; reloading and swapping them is very cumbersome.

no, what makes bioshock special are the moments of transcendence, when everything Just Works. when you hack a turret and then three rooms over an ‘enemy spotted’ timer pops up on your screen, knowing that when you backtrack you’re a bit more safer. when you hypnotize a big daddy and then manage to make your daddy fight another daddy. all the creepy ||living|| wax statues of fort frolic.

a capital G cynic might say that bioshock was the last dying gasp of a once glorious genre, watered down for consolites. i’d say bioshock proves that the spirit of these games is in the magic of letting things happen, even or sometimes because of restricted game mechanics, and that consoles or simplified game design really don’t have to be an encumbrance to that magic. perhaps in that way, ken levine has succeeded in his ultimate goal.

I remember the first time I played this: T'was the end of summer vacation and I was entering 7th grade in 2007. And in that most perilous gaming year of 07, that was the time I began to realize how my taste in games was truly being forged before my eyes. Playing games The Darkness, Gears of War, Call of Duty 2, Condemned and oh so much more were help defining what I love in video games and the next step in my journey was the tale of a destroyed Utopia in Irrational Games' seminal classic shooter Bioshock,

Even to this day, this thing still holds up really well: The chaotic combat that makes you act quick on your toes, the stellar sound design that heights the atmosphere to intoxicating levels, the dense level design that makes you look around every corner, the marvelous art direction that still holds your attention even if visually ir shows its age. But the thing that is the really big selling point here is it's story, a tale of madness, murder, obsession, cruelty, humanity, greed, deceit but maybe even hope...if you play your cards correctly. The voice work is of course exceptional (especially that Armin Shimerman's iconic Andrew Ryan) and the dialogue is so sharply written it could very easily be confused for a award winning novel than a video game from the 360 era, where edginess reigned supreme. And on top of that, the visuals do show their ages with things like the character models.

But ultimately, at the end of the day, this is a journey into a beautiful hell that is still worth taking. While we bemoan the presence of live service games or botched AAA launches with questionable writing, we can always come back (or dive in for the first time) to works such as these.
