Disclaimer: My playtime didn't register for reasons explained near the end of this review.
I actually completed the game twice (a Normal run with all audio logs and Little Sisters collected, and a Hard run with Vita Chambers disabled), so I know more than enough about this game to make a proper review of it.

Welcome to Rapture, a once thriving underwater city that fell to insanity and complete chaos after its inhabitants got addicted to ADAM, a substance granting super-powers and enhanced healing capabilities. You play as Jack, the token silent dood who's unlucky enough to plane crash in the middle of the sea and find himself in Rapture in the aftermath of the war confronting Andrew Ryan, the visionary leader of Rapture, to Atlas and his band of rebels, who are desperately struggling to stop Ryan's madness. From there, you'll embark on a grim journey in the depths of the ocean, fighting your way through underwater buildings and corridors infested with the deranged splicers, as well as the infamous Big Daddies, pedophiles in diving suits moaning like whales and stalking 8-year old little girls with giant syringes and glowing eyes.

Without spoiling anything, the story of the game is interesting and complex enough (for a FPS) to follow till the end, with its fair share of plot twists and excellent voice acting, although the endings were in my opinion slightly disappointing. Visually, the game aged quite well and the various steampunk environments of Rapture are a real treat to explore, which you'll have to do if you're interested in the background story of the city, distilled through audio logs scattered around the levels. The musical score is quite discreet but comes at the right moments, and the soundscape is well done. Atmosphere-wise, the game clearly takes inspirations from classics like System Shock 2 (the insane splicers from BioShock and the enraged infected from System Shock share some similarities) and the game certainly got its lots of creepy moments, from your first encounter with the splicers to your stroll through the medical ward, without forgetting your stay in Fort Frolic, the depraved home of the equally depraved Sander Cohen. Don't expect however visceral horror that will make you soil your pants as you would in games like Outlast or DreadOut. BioShock barely rely on jump scares or stuff of the sort, and while there's gory scenery here and there, the fear it tries to instill is more subtle, often mixing the awe-inspiring marvels of Rapture with a dose of creepiness to strike a chord of the uneasy kind.

Gameplay-wise, I'd hardly say the game has RPG elements, unless you count ADAM as experience points. However, it allows you to customize your experience in three different ways: Plasmids, Tonics, and weapons. Plasmids are kind of the equivalent of spells and come in many sorts (elemental attacks, ability to create a decoy or to mind control a Big Daddy to make it temporarily your ally...) - you use a "mana" bar (EVE) to use them, and you acquire most of them by spending the ADAM you will collect from the Little Sisters you encounter in the various levels. Tonics are passive abilities that you can equip on your character to give yourself various bonuses (see that as rings or amulets maybe?). You can find many hidden off the beaten trail in the levels, while others are bought with ADAM or offered as rewards for performing certain actions in the game. Finally, there is a variety of different weapons which all come with three types of different ammunitions whose effectiveness act on a rock-paper-scissors basis on ennemies depending on their weaknesses. You can also enhance permanently your weapons in different ways in specific stations scattered throughout the game which can be used only once for each. There are some other ways to customize your character, as ADAM also allows you to buy more Plasmid or Tonic slots to equip them, and to increase your Health or EVE bar. Later in the game is also introduced a crafting system were you can create your own ammo with materials you find on ennemies or in containers.

Now if we have to talk about the flaws, I'd say there are two main ones in this game. The first is that you're actually more limited than you think when it comes to customization. You'll quickly learn that some Plasmids and Tonics are must-haves, while others are completely useless (I'm looking at you, Natural Camouflage), which substantially reduces your options, as a lot of Plasmids and Tonics also have synergies between them. Same goes for the weapons: I found myself never using certain types of weapons or ammunitions because they proved utterly ineffective even when fully upgraded compared to other ones, and the weapon enhancing part with the previously mentioned stations also only gives you the illusion of choice, as you will eventually get all the upgrades anyways if you manage to find them all (which isn't that hard). It only comes down to which ones you take first. The second flaw for me is that the difficulty wasn't balanced very well. The game can be excessively hard and unfair during the first half of the game (this is especially true on Hard), with some ennemies being huge bullet sponges and hitting like trucks while your own options are very limited. But by the time you reach the second half of the game (around the end of Fort Frolic, beginning of Hephaestus) and have accumulated enough Plasmids, Tonics and research on ennemies, you'll often find yourself not being able to loot ammo or money because you have already plenty of them, to a point where I ended up just hacking everything I was coming across with money or auto-hack because hacking the regular way was getting too dull after the 150th time (one other small flaw I should have mentioned).

I would however say the pros of this game make up for the aforementioned cons. It was a very enjoyable ride that can still hold up to the current gen FPS, which I'm not sure is saying a lot considering today's low standards. If you have a taste for story-driven FPS with an interesting setting, great atmosphere and enjoyable gameplay, you should definitely play to BioShock. 
Brotip: If you're going to do only one playthrough, try to save all the Little Sisters. I can assure you you'll find the ending much more satisfying than the other one.

Why a negative review then? More explanations below.
Should a "Neutral" review button had been available, I would have gone for that actually, but I just can't press "Yes" for the following reason.

This game is old, and isn't meant to be played on systems beyond Windows Vista. For those still running on Vista or older, then consider that review a definitive Yes. But if you're running on Windows 7 and above, the game crashes constantly (or doesn't launch, plain and simple), to the point you'll spend more time watching the opening logos than actually playing the game, and the ways to fix this can greatly vary for one system to another. As far as I'm concerned, I had to mess with the .exe file in the game folder and launch the game through it. Adding the .exe to my Steam library as a non-Steam game worked, but the Steam overlay had to be deactivated as it would also make the game crash. So my registered playtime is only the time I spent struggling to reach the end of the first area with a crash every 2 minutes. 

If like me, you waited way too long to play this game and are considering whether you should buy it or not, I'm warmly encouraging you to give it a go. You won't regret it. But not on Steam. The Steam version doesn't have any extra feature you could possibly miss.

I played this game much later in its life span, so I missed its “glory days.” What I experienced was a game very much of its time, with all the hallmarks, and frustrations, of games from that era. The pacing didn’t match how I personally like to play; the story didn’t develop in a way that kept me engaged at my pace, and the world, full of collectables and exploration, sometimes felt tedious. Inventory limits meant I could carry 500 spoons but struggle with more practical items, which highlighted the game’s focus on immersion and depth rather than streamlined action.

Looking back, my frustration came less from the game failing and more from my own expectations. This isn’t a twitch shooter; it’s a deep RPG emphasizing exploration, and by design, it rewards patience and curiosity. While it may not have aligned with my play style, it’s undeniably a well-crafted game. My reaction is more about the conflict between my current perspective and how I imagine I would have enjoyed it at the time, rather than an indictment of the game itself. In short: it’s good, just not for me.

Ah, the original Bioshock, a festering cesspool of disappointment and incompetence. Let's start with the gameplay, shall we? It's about as enjoyable as a rectal exam administered by a blindfolded chimpanzee in a dark alley. The controls, oh sweet Lord, the controls! They're more convoluted than a politician's excuse for laundering money. Trying to maneuver through the twisted corridors of Rapture is like trying to guide a drunken elephant through a china shop during an earthquake. And don't even get me started on the combat; it's like trying to punch your way out of a wet paper bag with a limp noodle while blindfolded and handcuffed.

Now, onto the story. Oh, what a steaming pile of pretentious nonsense it is! The so-called "twists" are about as surprising as finding a cockroach in your kitchen. And the narrative? It's like watching paint dry while listening to a cat being strangled by a rusty trombone. The characters are as shallow as a puddle in the Sahara, and the plot holes are bigger than the craters on the moon. It's like the writers got together and said, "Let's see how many clichés we can cram into one game and call it groundbreaking."

And let's not forget about the PC port, a flaming dumpster fire of incompetence and laziness. The controls are about as responsive as a stone statue, and the optimization is so poor that even a potato could run circles around it while laughing hysterically. It's like they took a masterpiece and smeared it with the feces of a diseased rat, then lit it on fire and threw it off a cliff.

In conclusion, Bioshock is a prime example of everything wrong with modern gaming. It's a bloated, pretentious mess that's about as enjoyable as a root canal without anesthesia while being serenaded by a choir of tone-deaf banshees. From elsewhere: 
Bioshock, when first released, had a lot of buzz. I was kinda excited as previews and reviewers mentioned a somewhat RPG-styled FPS much like Deus Ex.

Playing through it several times (I've put well over 50 hours), I can easily summarize the game as just a mediocre FPS. Harsh? Compared to how nice everyone else is to this game, yeah, but I think it's a more objective view.

Before we read a laundry list of what could have been differently we should examine what this game does right: atmosphere. The maps, the lighting, the sound, the contents of the recordings, and the art design (a very retro futuristic style that made the first Fallout so memorable). Exploring the Rapture was great fun for the first time, but very linear. Yes, there are things you can miss on the sides one your first play through, but it doesn't effect the game at all. But that should be expected from a decent shooter. Of course any sense of dread is not to be found as the fear of dying in this game is non existent. 

The plasmids are kinda like augments of Deus Ex, in that when applied, they may change the style in which you play the game. Not by much, and in fact, disregard the notion of it changing your play style. They're nothing special, and the only one mildly entertaining to use is telekinesis (which behaves like the gravity gun of Half-Life 2). 

Combat feels kinda sloppy and not as responsive as, for example TF2 or Borderlands, as the enemies (being poorly animated) move very awkwardly in a jerky motion. It's not the worst, but the weapons don't feel as responsive as they should (aside from the shotgun and wrench).

The game overall isn't anything special; how could it have been better?

For one, more vents/alternative routes. This could do more for a stealthy play through than Decoy and Chameleon plasmids.

Make character development through plasmids a little more permanent. By this I mean, when changing your DNA, whatever is added can't be undone, and no swapping with the gene banks. Also beyond that, they should have made different paths for builds, like when choosing one plasmid you open the way for one group but close your way to other ones (and of course increase the number of plasmids as well). This would make how you spend your Adam more interesting.

One the same theme as plasmids, weapon upgrades feel bleh. It felt stupid that by the end of the game all of the weapons you found could be upgraded completely. A better solution would have been to follow the same route as the proposed plasmid upgrades: have way more options but not all of them selectable as the choices you make affect the upgrades that can be made. And since you'll almost always have 500 dollars on hand, why not make the upgrades cost something? 

The amount you could carry followed the same issue with everything else in the game: you can do everything! This means, at any point in the game you could switch to any weapon and meet any situation. If there were limitations to how many weapons and ammo you could carry and with numerous weapon mods available, the game would be more interesting, have better replay ability.

Playing BioShock now reminded me how I forced myself to like it when it came out - possibly because I had bought a new GPU specifically for this game and everyone was raving about it.

The environment of the underwater city is still absolutely phenomenal and the graphics hold up pretty well even after 14 years. The story is also interesting, if a little heavy-handed, but the gameplay... God it's such a repetitive and unsatisfying shooter. Then there's a lot of pointless looting for crumbs and that goddamn hacking minigame. Even the game is aware how annoying the "hacking" is and offers you to bypass it by "buying out".

BioShock may look like an "immersive sim", but in fact it's just a really dumb shooter. An iconic one, but still, the story alone isn't worth suffering through the game.

I know I'm not going to like a game when I quit playing and just go read the plot synopsis on Wikipedia.  It took me a few times to realize why I don't recommend this game.

Spoilers follow unapologetically.  Also, just so it's out of the way, the graphics are pretty good, for what that's worth.

The story and premise are ridiculous.  Someone I'm assuming is a multi-quintillionaire in 1950s money decides to start an underwater objectivist cult (Ayn Rand, for those who don't know what objectivism means), build a replica of Manhattan at the bottom of the sea, call it "Rapture" (which is a Bible thing, not a philosophy thing--but the irony of a rich man's "Rapture" underwater was amusing at least), and then basically manipulate whatever white people (yeah, they're all white, so far as I could tell) decide to come down to "escape" from the oppression on the surface.  That was probably a cool idea for a silent film back in 1910, but not today.  The story starts off with a guy in a plane, who presumably blows up the plane due to hypnosis, survives the otherwise totally fatal plane crash, and...lo and behold, managed to do all of this next to a lighthouse in the middle of the Atlantic, which turns out to be the only access point for the underwater city.  The odds of being on the right plane over the right spot in the Atlantic at the right time, and the malevolence required to blow a plane up for the purpose of being "inserted" into the undersea adventure...I'm sorry, but it's absurd, and TERRIBLE writing.

Gameplay is mediocre.  Bullets don't hurt people much, but a wrench will kill them instantly.  The vending machines in the game are basically there for the convenience of people shooting each other to solve problems, or for our wonderful adventure.  Hacking them is supposed to make things cheaper, but it doesn't.  Hacking other devices is often useful, and the minigame will keep players on edge to complete it, but that's actually the scariest part of the game.  There's a lot of gore and some body horror, but nothing particularly scary.  Jump scares come in the form of respawning enemies who appear out of nowhere, effectively ruining any sense of progress--how cheap!

Don't pay more than $5 for this game.  It really doesn't live up to the hype or stand the test of time.  I might finish it to say I did, but that's about it.  In final analysis, I think Bioshock Infinite is a total rewrite of this game, and is exponentially better, in all ways.  Go play that, before or after this one, and you'll see what I mean.

To tell you the truth, I can't say I understand why people praise this game so much. I really wanted to like the game, I really did, but I just couldn't.

So the story basically goes as follows: you survive a plane crash in the Atlantic. For some weird reason you step in a bathysphere and descend into a huge underwater city whose residents have gone insane because of some genetic alteration mumbo jumbo. Okay, so far the story sounds really cool and innovative, right? The concept becomes even cooler when you include the wacky 1960s style cultural and aesthetic theme which really reminds me of Fallout series.

Unfortunately, Bioshock kind of [b]wastes the massive potential[/b] of these ideas. The developers just don't seem to know how to tell a good story in a video game.

Good story needs exciting and preferably unexpected twists like loss of loved ones, betrayals, failures, rescues and such. It needs high and low points and should alternate between big emotions like love, hate, excitement, desperation, sadness etc. However this is not possible if the characters of the story are not interesting and important enough for you to care. For example, if you (the player) haven't had time to form [b]an emotional connection with a character[/b] whose death or betrayal is supposed to be dramatic, then it's [b]not going to affect you strongly.[/b]

I found myself asking myself [b]questions like "Why am I supposed to care?"[/b] over and over again. For most of the game your character doesn't even seem to have much personal connection to the things that are happening around him. It seems [b]he is just a bystander who got involved in someone else's war.[/b] In the end it turns out that he actually did have a personal connection but this comes [b]way too late to save the game[/b] and even then this "connection" turns out to be a very uninteresting.

I also can't understand why they had to do the silent protagonist thing, because it really doesn't add anything valuable to the story. Did the makers of this game think that Half-Life was successful because Gordon Freeman is [b]a soulless and emotionless silent killing machine[/b] who doesn't even blink an eye to horrible things happening around him?

Besides that, there are a number of other story related problems. The storytelling is [b]monotonous[/b] as 90% of it is someone talking to you in a radio or voice logs. That's just cheap and [b]unimaginative[/b]. You don't even meet these other characters face to face except only few times.

[b]The protagonist is uninteresting as **** and the other characters are just shallow caricatures that try to be funny.[/b] On the other hand, the plot itself isn't that amazing either so the storytelling and characters aren't the only to blame.

The ending was also not that great. Only positive thought about it in my head was "Well at least it's over and I can go play something more interesting."

I could try to forgive the story if the game mechanics were strong enough. Sadly they are not. There are a few unusual mechanics (for FPS games) like throwing lightning bolts of your hand, kind of a skill management system, mini games and actually having to conserve your ammo and other supplies a bit. [b]I'm still not going to call that innovative, because it's not. This is not the first time in the history of shooter games you can pull magic tricks and don't have unlimited ammo.[/b]

Still, the mechanics are [b]kind of cool but just not enough to save the game[/b]. The shooting gets soon [b]really repetive[/b]. Your enemies just walk around shooting at you and you in fact do the exactly same. It's like a Team Fortress 2 game, instead of taking cover and doing careful decisions, you just run and jump around. If they had thrown in some breathtaking adrenaline pumping action sequences or more focus on stealth, perhaps this had still made a decent game. Now it isn't much above the boring mainstream of first person shooters. The biggest difference is that health isn't regenerating.

At least the city looks visually quite cool.

[b]There are a lot of games which have done storytelling right[/b], like Tomb Raider (2013), GTA 4, Last of Us, Alan Wake, Half-Life, The Walking Dead, Max Payne (1&2)... [b]BioShock just isn't one of them.[/b] I just wish the makers had had more ambition, courage and expertise to make BioShock as epic as it deserves to be.

> Example; the respawn mechanic taking away your acquired things that you have used would be fine. Ie, you resurrect in your last saved spot but minus anything you have used since. A perfect example of beautiful idea and poor execution. Bioshock manages to really wow with its graphics, animations and water effects unseen before. Despite its prowess in these areas the game proves that it is more style than substance as the player is constantly thrust into a reptitve slog of combat moving from one locked area to the next. Now to say that the combat is not fun would be doing this game a disservice, but once you have used all the gadgets and have fought all the enemies in the same manner for two hours it does not impress anymore. There is not enough variety to the gameplay here as you explore the mysterious city. The gameplay mechanics do not evovle or add to the FPS genre in an engaging way like Half-Life or Portal. The lack of proper pacing here makes every session a drag, especially if you decide to finish the game in one fell swoop. 

The story in the game is commendable, but given everything you hear in the logs it frankly leaves too much to the imagination and you cannot help but feel that it would have been more fun to play during the downfall rather than coming in well after the collapse. The voice actors do a good job of keeping you engaged, but their faceless characters like the story logs make it difficult to sympathise with their plight. This makes the connection feel very weak and keeping track of them all a chore as the cast builds over time. The idea to keep the player in the game rather than interrupting the gameplay with story cutscenes was a good one, however with the amount of information thrown at the player it simply does not work.

As universally lauded as this title, the flaws are overlooked by most. In a genre where innovative gameplay and impeccable story-telling are key to differentiate from the over-saturated market Bioshock does little to shake the foundations.

A lot of my friends and colleagues recommended Bioshock to me since I liked action horror games (like Resident Evil 4) and RPG FPS (like Borderlands). The critics of this game are overwhelmingly good, with a Metascore of 96.

But I don't like Bioshock.

The story seems interesting at first (under the sea, steam punk style, mad inhabitants of a once flourishing city of progress and freedom) and the sound and graphics quality is quite good. More than once I got a racing heart when an enemy lurked around the corner.

The voice quality (English and German synchro) is quite good, if not a little too polished and "clean". The options you have for customizing are pretty good, also the different ammunitions of your weapons add to the rock-paper-scissors gameplay of enemy strengths and weaknesses.

After a while, the game gets boring, though. The story – albeit twisted and unique – gets predictable, the "escape and save the world" tunnel view gives you a feel of limitation. Sure, you can't really expect an open world masterpiece from a game so old, but there were a lot of games with more linear levels which were still more interesting to play.

The enemy types repeat themselves over and over again. After the thirty-third Rosie and the sixhundredth small guy who you have to kill because he respawned and you can't just run past them, you just don't want to kill anything anymore. Which is bad for a first person shooter.

I always play on the hardest difficulty for a challenge, since most of the games nowadays are too easy. Bioshock however isn't _hard_ on the "hard" setting, it's just unfair. I never had the impression I could've killed all the enemies of one floor without dying; sometimes you just run into a horde of enemies or a mean trap and die in less than two seconds. Even Dark Souls made that better, there you always have the feeling you could have beaten this enemy if you were just better at blocking or similar.

I might continue this review when I have played the game through. This could take a while, since I don't enjoy this game a few hours in.

While people sing BioShock's praises, I'll have to wholeheartedly disagree with them. On one part, I do agree, the story is interesting and it's a shame that the other elements just don't do it justice.

The gameplay is... Just bad. The controls are clunky and counter intuitive, which leads to massive frustrations. A good example is when you fight the "Rosie" Big Daddy variants. These are long range types, who shoot at you with both a big-ass gun and grenades. One of the things your learn early on is "Use Telekinesis to throw the grenades back at the opponent". However, with this Big Daddy, you've got no chance of doing so.

For instance, if you keep your Telekinesis Plasmid active, it keeps on shooting its regular gun while you try to dodge the bullets to no success because for some reason, the bullets do still manage to hit you. When it finally DOES decide to throw a grenade, the Telekinesis Plasmid holds it in front of you (making it slightly see-through) but it still obscures the middle of the screen, making your throws INCREDIBLY innacurate.

If you manage to actually hit the Big Daddy and not something of the scenery (they're also "mine bombs", so when they land, they stay in place as a mine that can still hurt your ass which is so much fun...) the grenade does a marginally low amount of damage for the time that you've been shoving Med-Kits in your gaping wounds while jumping from side to side like a cartoon character that tries to dodge gunfire.

So, what do you do? You pull out your Tommy Gun to lay some smackdown on the mofo. You open fire, seeing that the damage you do is comparable to the damage an ant does to a plate of solid steel: almost jack-shit. However, for some reason, this makes the Big Daddy more inclined to throw grenades, so when you see the grenade fly towards you, you immediately go for your Telekinesis Plasmid and get hit in the face with the damn grenade. Wanna know why? THE PLASMIDS AREN'T ABLE TO BE ACTIVATED IMMEDIATELY! Yeah, so you see the grenade coming, you switch to the plasmid by pulling the left trigger, instinctively holding it because that'd make sense and activate the ability immediately, but no! It doesn't! You'd have to let go of the trigger first, then pull it again to activate the plasmid, hoping it does, but by the time it goes off, your ass is decorating several walls in the scenery already!

Another big problem: Enemies. Keep. Spawning. No matter what. Now, I'm a very thorough person, going through the entire map before heading to the objective marker because I want to explore every nook and cranny of the place and find everything that you can. However, this is hampered by enemies who suddenly appear out of fucking nowhere. Even though you've gone through the damn room 3 times already, there will ALWAYS be enemies that return. This takes away any sense of progression or accomplishment because it just makes you feel as if you're shoving your fingers in the holes in your boat to stop the leaking, and every time you close up one hole, another one pops up!

Compare this to Halo. In that, you'd murder an entire level and when you ran back for the supply drop you know you skipped on purpose to conserve ammo and grenades, you'd feel like an utter demon because, holy shit, you totally decimated their forces. Everything's dead, the place is silent, no suicide Grunts that pop out of nowhere, no Elites yelling "Wort Wort Wort" or anything. That made you feel awesome and creep you out because the levels felt so empty all of a sudden.

Here, you're backing up because a Big Daddy is closing in, only to get a grenade shoved up your ass by a guy who, logically, SHOULDN'T EVEN BE THERE!

Like, the Fishery level. You arrive there in a Bathysphere, the room you arrive in has no place for ANYONE to enter but through the bathysphere. You run through it, encounter your first Rosie Big Daddy, and you start backing up while firing your guns. All of a sudden, something explodes next to you, taking out a quarter of your health, and as you turn around, you realise that it's a damn fodder enemy that spawned in for the Hell of it. Good work there!

Then again, dying has no consequence either. With games like Halo, you're running when you're low on Health, hoping for that "Game Saved" pop up so you can keep your progress even if you die. Here, when you die, you just get back up, get to keep all your weapons, get to keep all your progression and most importantly you get to keep your enemy damage. So... Whatever, draw a Big Daddy to a Vita Chamber, then turn it into Swiss Cheese by turning into a steampunk version of Deadpool because you keep popping up without any repercussions.

Part of me is glad they did that, because if they didn't, this game would've been even worse than it is now...

As it stands, I don't see why people sing its praises so damn much. Sure, it's pretty, atmospheric and has a good story, but if the gameplay sucks, it's all for naught.

Bioshock 1 is one of the gaming legends of a few decades ago. A light immersive sim first person shooter with one of the best ambientations I've seen in a long while, Bioshock is in a lot of regards, a massively well thought out game. Both from the cultural landscape of the fictional city of rapture to the plotline and how it all connects together, all the parts related to the world building and story are honestly great and when looking in hindsight, it still looks like a masterpiece.

Gameplay-wise is where things get a bit funky. The moment to moment gameplay is not nearly as interesting as the world building around Rapture.

Weapons are varied and have their uses and that's honestly a huge plus and the many different plasmids -this game's special skills- offer many different playstyles. Shooting, using powers, hacking, using the environment to your advantage, the toolset the player has at their disposition is commendable.

The problem comes with the design of the enemies and environments themselves. One of the first and most prevalent problems in this game is that at all difficulties, someone will be a bullet sponge. Either enemies will be ridiculous bullet sponges tanking your entire ammo reserves in higher difficulties or you will be as tough as a big daddy on lower difficulties, making guns feel inconsistent and, honestly, weak in a lot of cases. Some might argue that's by design to encourage using plasmids more, but I'd rather have bullets be a more scarce resource (more rare and expensive) than having it just be weaker. Bullet sponges are not fun and gunfights with bullet sponges are historically boring.

The other major problem is, honestly, how linear the whole experience is. While I understand Bioshock is a linear experience going from point A to Point B, to have the design of the explorable city reflect that as well really makes Rapture feel much smaller and the invisible hand of the dev way more visible.

Finally, we have the morality system in this game. I understand it was novel at the time and making it a binary critical story decision was much easier to implement, but it falls really short really fast. The moral dillema without spoiling anything is basically the following: The oppresive environment of the broken rapture and the splicers running around, the city is extremely hostile and dangerous. In universe, the only way to survive is by getting plasmids to enhance your capacities because just being good with guns ain't gonna cut it. Then, you find a choice to do something immoral to get a bunch of ADAM, the resource you spend to get more plasmids. Or you can do the good thing and... still get almost as much adam as before? If not even more???? With Extra rewards???? I'm not even talking about the moral satisfaction of doing the right thing or the gratitude of people, I mean you probably get more resources by just doing the right thing, which ruins the in universe tension of doing said choice, because the immoral choice would ordinarily be counterweighter with the fact that it's the safer option for survival, while the good choice would be harder to make because instead of choosing convenience, you'd choose to care for someone in need. But it absolutely FUMBLES the concept by making the good route also have more rewards, making the bad ending just dumber in general.

Bioshock did a lot of things right. But as fate would have it, it also stumbled a lot. I tried to finish it several times, but never could finish it. Thinking about the game was always a lot cooler than actually playing it.

I recognize the historical value this game has, but ultimately, I feel the mythos of the game and its legacy are grander than the game itself.

One of the most fantastic but frustrating games I have ever played.

To start off, the game is fantastic in the sense that 2K & Irrational games have created a game that is truly unique and vastly different than any other game at the time.  Almost 10 years later, Bioshock has aged very well and can easily be played for many more years to come.  The weapons & combat system offer great variety and satisfaction.  Shooting an enemy with a pistol to taking photos of hideous splicers for damage buffs, each weapon offers something unique for every combat situation as well as enjoyability.  

Visually, Bioshock is beautiful; considering it's age, the graphic design really is ground breaking compared to many other games that were made of the same year.  There are many small details that Irrational games added to give a strong emotional feel towards Rapture - the environment and atmosphere in particular.  The water and fire effects are pleasing to look at.  I believe the graphics in Bioshock will withstand the test of time.

The story is very well done.  From beginning to end you will most definitely be engaged,  I don't want to put any spoilers on this review so I will keep this part short; the game's story is very good.

Now,  this is the kicker for this game - not the game in particular, but, STEAM's version of the game.  There are MAJOR MAJOR MAJOR bug issues with this game on STEAM.  First of all, you cannot play this game without a microphone plugged in; don't even bother starting it up because you're game is just going to crash before you even hit the main menu.  

The next part is where Bioshock on STEAM will make you drop to your knees and cry.  The game WILL CRASH ON YOU.  I have tried everything in my power to make this game fully operational but nothing worked.  I had to save this game EVERY 30 seconds to a minute.  Since Bioshock does NOT have autosave you have to do it yourself; guess what happens when you forget to save the game? That's correct! You lose all your progress! YAY!

I somehow managed to finish this game, considering how much I enjoyed it while it managed to run for 10-15 minutes at a time before I had to reboot it.  If you can withstand this kind of frustration and headache then you will love this game - otherwise, just buy an XBOX 360 and play this game on the console.

5/5 Gameplay, Graphics and Story

Bioshock pisses me off. I found this game irritating from the very beginning and I'm not interested in playing the rest of it. I'll even tell you exactly where and why I stopped playing.

Like almost everyone, I bought all 3 Bioshock games in a bundle for a very low price during a steam sale. I also bought System Shock 2. I skipped the first System Shock due to its widely known reputation for being user unfriendly. Otherwise, I planned to play them in order.

System Shock 2 is a compelling game with real grit to its mechanics and overall design, so that went fine. I was convinced I was making all the big brain plays, because System Shock 2 makes you feel like you're outsmarting the game. Thematically, System Shock 2 is also a game about outsmarting a computer, making for a cohesive experience which evokes a particular feeling.

Bioshock is like playing with action figures. I was already familiar with "console shooters" such as Turok, Goldeneye 007 and Time Splitters, but what those games lacked in mechanical depth they made up for in charm. If I were to describe Bioshock in a single word, it would be Sluggish.

Bioshock is slow. The character you play as walks slowly. He shoots slowly, reloads slowly, injects healing stims slowly, and harvest the souls of little girls even more slowly than he shoots, reloads, injects or walks. Don't worry, they're not really little girls and it's not really "their souls". The visual design of the game seems to be inspired by the Clayfighters franchise. Deformed and shapeless blobs everywhere. Even flat walls evade the quality of appearing to be walls. It's all the crazy shit hanging off of them, I think (Shenanigans)

Compared to Metroid Prime and Metroid Prime 2, where optional logs give the impression professional writers might have been involved, the writing in Bioshock is an absolute mess. Aside from world building, the quality of the writing signalled towards the intended audience for Metroid: not exclusively children, maybe? The optional logs in Bioshock are "juvenile" and "indistinguishable from the work of an edgy teen." The audio is equally obnoxious. While probably fine on a television soundsystem, on headphones it is cluttered and claustrophobia inducing. 

Everything about this game is goddamn irritating at the most basic level before you even get to what it feels like playing it. The first area is a tutorial area, and is predictably basic. There is one off the beaten track segment guarded by security cameras where an upgrade is hidden, but the upgrade is required to complete the level so there's nothing special about finding it. There's also a moment where the game throws more enemies at you at one time than it has up to that point, but the audio cue announcing their arrival is obvious enough there's plenty of time to formulate a plan, like cheesing the wave by backing into the farthest corner and picking them off as they run at you single file. This feels suitably "video game-y" and gave me a feeling of satisfaction. The level is capped off when you butt heads with a Big Daddy. There's only one viable way of taking this guy down since the game hasn't given you very many resources at this point. Electrify the Big Daddy, blast into it with armour piercing bullets until the beast is about the shake off the electricity, then shock it again and repeat. Like applying shampoo. The choice of whether to off the "little sister" or save her has the emotional weight of a brick. Oh it's heavy, in a bland obvious way. By the time you do this for the 8th time it will have lost any meaning at all.

The second area is a big improvement on the first. The walls in this area have a more wall-like quality, with more structure and therefore more personality as you can actually memorize it fairly easily by walking through it a couple of times. Memorization is important in this game as the ingame map is worse than useless. The different rooms here are also distinct and memorable. There's a freedom of choice in which direction the player heads in first and the pacing is fantastic, somewhat frantic if you want it to be or slower if you prefer but the frequency of obstacles and problems to solve to dead space is about right. 

The third area is where Bioshock takes a serious nosedive and its where I've stopped playing not once, but twice. Yes I installed the game, played to the third area, lost interest, uninstalled the game, waited a couple years, gave it another try from the beginning and lost interest again in the exact same spot. The third area of Bioshock is an amorphous vomit puddle out of nowhere. If I were a professional game critic, I would force myself through this and hopefully enjoy the rest of the game. But I'm not a professional critic and I'm not going to force myself through this and hopefully enjoy the rest of the game, I'm going to uninstall and give it another try in a couple years.

2 things I enjoyed:
- Big Daddys don't aggro you, making all Big Daddy fights completely optional. This is a real choice which makes a difference to the player experience, unlike the "do u want to kill girl for upgrade points lol" choice which is completely vapid and meaningless. The Big Daddys and Little Sisters feel like a distinct faction, because they behave differently from the splicers who always attack on sight. Half-Life tackled the idea of factions before this but in the end if either faction saw you, they'd attack, making them not functionally different. The "Hypnotize Big Daddy" powerup makes a lot more sense because of this, too.
- Some of the in-jokes were funny to me, and there are a lot of in-jokes which might be why game critics slobbered all over this games big fat d. The pointlessly silly and tonally out of place hacking mini-game is as tedious as it is funny, and it's funny as shit.

As quite a lot of people have mentioned, Bioshock has not aged well. The games does work on Windows 7 64 bit (the os I ran it on) but I had to do a bit of tweaking to get it stable, for instance, I had to run it in Dx9 mode. With Vsync on the game suffers from frequent slowdowns and stutter (with i5 3570k and hd7950) and if you have the mouse sensitivity on low, the in game menus are near impossible to navigate. Turning off Vsync will alleviate these problems but you will get a lot of screen tearing.

The game itself is an interesting idea but suffers from a poor user interface, the environments all look pretty much the same and the objectives are mostly 'kill something and collect items from corpse'. This involves lots of random searching for enemies in the hope they might hold the item you need. You can also 'hack' certain things in the game (security systems, vending machines etc) but the hacking game is so annoying that I didnt bother for the entire game, I just used the auto hacking tool.

Overall, the game was fairly enjoyable in spite of all the flaws, this was helped by the interesting story and freaky characters. If you can put up with all the flaws I am sure you will get some enjoyment out of this but as a full price release I cannot recommend it.

The game's settings were the biggest con for me. They are outdated, console centered, and they don't even save sometimes. Even after directly editing the config file and setting it as read only, it still defaulted, although not immediately. Other than that, the physics have a low frame rate so objects that are spinning and falling look derpy. And as with all Bioshock games, it can get a bit grindy sometimes. This games graphics did not age as well as games like HL2, particularly in the bumpmapping area. In the possitive aspects, the gameplay was very fun, the story line was great (and i reccomend it if you're going to play Burial at Sea), and the ending was good as well. There's a large variety of weapons so you have many ways to play and the game even leaves you with a few moral choices. I was able to run this on Max graphics on a video card with 1G of memory. Overall, the settings and the fact that my progress was not saved somehow (I may have uninstalled the game, should have backed the save up) led me to just watch a walkthrough on youtube to see the last third of the game. Should you get this game? It depends on if you're the type of person who will play Portal 1 before Portal 2; the storyline is so simple in Portal 1 and most of the time spent playing is spent playing a game mechanic: puzzles with portals. I can't stress enough how many things are wrong with this game. Don't get me wrong, it can be enjoyable, but it's worthless.
First of all, dying. You've got two possibilities. Either you let the game work on its defaults and be worthless and boring or you get utterly annoyed. By default everytime you die you respawn in the nearest booth. You loose some cash and that's all. This means that there's close to none penalty for dying. You just kill the remaining enemies and go on, there will be even more money later.
Now what if you turn that feature off? Well, first you need to know that you can. There's no info or tip about it, there's no telling the player in the tutorial part, that player can turn that off. You have to open the settings menu and find it on your own. Then disable it.
At this point let me remind you this game is using GFWL system, which is the worst kind of RDM I have ever seen in my life. All the files must be verified and synchronised with the cloud server, this means you cannot access your saves in offline mode, autosaves go there too, and worst of all, they have to load everytime you do something. You're in a menu? Three seconds of freeze so it can verify if you're logged in. Opening single player? Another three seconds of the same. Opening loading menu? Another 5 seconds of downloading your saves. Then you load the game and wait for it to load.
And that's the problem. When you die without respawn "feature" you do not get the last save loaded automatically, or loading screen opened. No - you get kicked out to the main menu. Getting through all the verifications, loading the saves and loading the selected save, everytime you die you loose 30-40 seconds of your life. Be in a tough moment of game and in 12 minutes you spend 9 loading the game and 3 trying to beat that hard part. I really cannot say how very bad that is.
What next? The difficulty.
When I said "hard part" before I meant "one of the three moments in the whole game IF you've chosen "hard" difficulty and turned respawns off". If you didn't there are no hard moments since you just go back there and kill whoever killed you. If anybody killed you. Unless you're on hard it's hard to get killed.
Whole game is generaly pointless, worthless and meaningless, because player is godmoded, spoiled kid that never gets punished for anything.
Speaking of anything - you can't change anything despite illusion of choice. You either save or kill little girls, harvesting power from them(gruesome, isn't it?), you get less of it if you save them, but the only reason to save them is so you can feel good about yourself getting a little nicer ending where instead of lying in hospital bed alone, you lie in hospital bed with some girls holding your mutated, ugly, old hand. Game took me 12 hours on hard with respawns off, it's not rewarding.

There's nice plot twist, though. But that's the only good side of it.

The game is interesting and innovative, speaking of shooting along with superpower, Bioshock is still one of the few games that matters. But this first game in franchise does give me so many problems compared to the third game Infinite. It is the first time I understand the importance of balance.

Minor Control Issue. We have to switch powers and guns instead of duel, it is the biggest flaw when it comes to basic control. It's not good but considering the tech problem is somehow hard to solve back to the days, I say it is only a minor issue after I get used to it.

And something I can't get used to is the game balance. I can't enjoy the game until the last few levels because the resources and abilities are so limited.

First few levels, I spend all the time collecting ammo, and even have some spare loot, but I don't dare to shoot Big Daddy because it is too hard even in normal difficulty, Mr.B can kill us in two shots. It is just torture, I have to leverage the environment like gun turret and oil drums. And guess what, after neptune's bounty, the ammo I struggle to save is robbed, fine, it is the setting, but why all special ammo is gone? I find people experiencing the same problems and someone says the remastered version has fixed this problem, haha, such big bug is not on their bug list until they need to milk new money.

I keep moving. The atmosphere is scary, enemies do scream and also make sound of footstep. I am sensitive to sound, such design is a little annoying because early days the sound design is not precise and distant sound could confuse me it is close. But the real problem is still lack of resources, or being afraid to use because we don't know whether we can survive later. The stifling game experience makes me decide to change my tactic, I should believe the game and have fun, enjoy the fight, well, the ammo indeed is not the problem, I don't have enough life. A big dilemma.

In another immersive sim Dishonored, where similarly we have to collect resources and keep saving progress, after I work hard on collecting, I can go with either assassination or fight, I have the confidence and I do enjoy it, I will not be reduced to a situation where I have no ammo or life.

Still, trust the game and carry on, finally after 20 hours, after enough upgrade and camera research, the enemies are not lethal anymore, I can actually see there is a way to do. This game costs me too much patience in the early stage, even more than Witcher 3. When I start to enjoy it, 30 hours has past, and there's only three levels left, the fun of exploration is gone because my resources are barely consumed.

In general, the game has no adaptive phase for players, we have to accept the harsh challenges and bear it, we survive as the protagonist does, it is pretty good in the term of immersive sim, but I don't enjoy such design, Tomb Raider is also a game where we start from the ground zero, but the challenge starts with a feasible level. The key difference is the irrational resource design, we are supposed to have more resources when we are weak, not after we are full of everything.

This game didn't work for me. 
It sounded very promising: a mysterious city at the bottom of the ocean, a universe based on Ayn Rand's works and taking it to the extreme, a world that's essentially become a big psycho asylum... But to be honest, everything about this game felt rushed. It made me feel like I was playing a draft. From the approximative story that makes you ask yourself unwanted questions all the time to the lack of attention to detail (at some point you have to operate a machine and the needles on the gauges were moving like goddamn windshield wipers, it really threw me off), I didn't experience any real immersion; ironic for a game that takes place under the sea. 
The splicers all have the same moving pattern, with that jump when they get at melee distance which looks great in the beginning but gets old really fast. And they're too grotesque to be actually scary. Most of the voice acting is sub-par, and the fact that basically all the characters have thick accents and use a lot of obscure slang didn't help anything. The only character that felt real to me was McDonagh. Shame that you don't even get to meet him. The plasmids are great, but the fact that you can't wield one in your left hand while wielding a handgun or your wrench in your right hand seemed like wasted potential to me. 

Basically there are two types of good game scenarios: the ones that explain pretty much nothing and let you make up the story in your head using some subtle hints, and the ones that explain about everything, leaving you with satisfying answers to your questions. Falling right in between these two, Bioshock's scenario failed to hook me up. Even the "twist" was utterly predictable and pretty obvious since the beginning. And the ending is particularly anticlimatic.

Sure, the game looks good. Sure, it has its fair share of originality. But it's also very, very repetitive, and when you're not having fun... It made me wish that you gained XP for killing the damn splicers! Something that had never happened to me in a FPS before.

Possibly one of the worst games I've played.

The story tried to be complex or deep but failed. It's cliche with twists I spotted a mile away. I started counting the tropes. The only thing that was remotely interesting was finding out the origin of the protagonist. Otherwise, narration is redundant information through shitty radio monologues. 

The gameplay is awful. Gunplay is atrocious, poorly-planned, and frustrating. I understand ammo management is an element of the thriller genre, but dealing with it across 8-9 weapons with three ammo types each causes fights to devolve into scrolling through weapons for a bullet to load and fire. This is simply poor game design. The enemies you fight are extremely homogenous. They all jump around, tank bullets, and succumb to the same repetition of plasmids/wrenching. Sometimes they have guns that they mag-dump into a wall you're behind. Of course they're only carrying one bullet when you kill them. They spawn in non-sense locations just to make it seem like you never have a break, which ruins the immersion. 

Player customization is also subpar - the abilities you earn through Adam are underpowered and unappealling. I stopped caring about customization when I realized it had no affect on my experience whatsoever. The role-playing game elements failed: there were no roles to be had - no investment in a playstyle - leaving the game an FPS with the usual two or three engagement tactics. 

The missions are almost all fetch quests - the most uninspired task you could assign a FPSRPG player. Only you have the willpower to walk all over town picking up junk for rewardless progression. Also prominent are "enemies flooding the room" defense tasks and the occasional escort mission. The landmark missions staked in this mire are best described as "flip this switch / push this buttion to hear more story".

The only thing this game has going for it is it's atmosphere. No, not even it's horrid map design, just the atmosphere of the environment.

The gameplay and mechanics in this game have not aged well compared to the sequel Bioshock 2 which has aged perfectly. This game does feel like a more casual version of System Shock 2. The only thing that holds up is the characters, story, atmosphere, political themes, and game world. The gameplay, shooting, and physics are clunky.  The hacking with the pipes are a chore! I recommend Bioshock 2 for its amazing gameplay, hacking system, and dual wielding gunplay. What ruins this game for me is the stupid ass pipe hacking minigame everytime you hack something gave me PTSD and I would stay the hell away from this game because of it! The hacking system in the sequel is a God send literally! Game is full of anti Capitalism and anti Ayn Rand themes. God I hate that bitch Ayn Rand. Andrew Ryan is both the heart and soul of this game. Without him Bioshock would have been a dull experience. Atlas is an amazing character and I won't spoil the plot but there is a twist that nobody! I mean nobody saw coming! Atlas is a supposed "Socialist Revolutionary and champion of the workers" fighting against the rich and privileged and Andrew Ryan is a anti Socialist and pro capitalist cynical man who hates the Governments of the surface world and wanted to create a underwater "utopia" where he could create a society that could be "free" from the influences of corrupt Government whether it was the United States or the Soviet Union! I'd still easily recommend Bioshock 2 over this! The FOV in this is restricted and it's way too zoomed in. What kept me playing through this was characters like Andrew Ryan, Sander Cohen, and others who were so charming and written so well that it made me forget all the fetch quests, backtracking, and those stupid hacking pipe minigames! The forced FOV makes this really frustrating to play while at least in the remaster you can change it to something more playable. Also in the remaster, they did add a new game plus mode which includes all your weapons, upgrades, plasmids, tonics, and money in a new playthrough.

In retrospect, the amount of baffling design decisions here is staggering. For one thing, the game is incredibly easy, even on the hardest difficulty, mainly due to there being quite literally no punishment for death. All that really happens is a few seconds of wasted time walking back to where you were killed. This creates a ridiculous combat loop of bullet sponge enemies that run to the nearest health station as soon as their HP is low enough, every single time, resulting in an irritating game of chasing them down which in turn leads you to a room full of enemies that'll melt your health pool in seconds and send you back to the nearest respawn point, repeat ad nauseum.

This dead horse of a point has already been beaten time and time again since 2007, but it really can't be overstated how absolutely awful the overabundance of hacking mini-games is. All I'll say is that it's kinda hilarious how the game gives you multiple ways to bypass doing them altogether, showing how confident 2K was that players would hate this aspect of the game. Plus, the poor sound mixing means it's quite often difficult to tell what's being said during the numerous voice logs throughout the game, meaning you'll likely have to turn on subtitles. Confusingly, doing so will only clutter your view with the greyed-out subtitle box that takes up nearly half the screen!

On top of all of this, the game treats you like someone who's never played a video game in their life, constantly bombarding you with obvious tips every minute right up until the credits roll. Yeah, I know I'm currently riddling the final boss with a barrage of bullets and lightning bolts, but it's good to be reminded that I can always search for loot in desks and trash cans when I'm running low on resources! Also, any time you need a certain ability to get somewhere, there's almost always a plasmid-changing station nearby, meaning there's basically no consequence for whatever loadout you decide to go with.

The storyline of the game is pretty good, despite 2K consistently beating you over the head with its themes of capitalism and hubris throughout, and occasionally trite dialogue. The synergy of plasmids in combat can be fun, and the final boss isn't nearly as bad as some people claim. Despite the handful of positives Bioshock offers, I can't forgive the abysmal map, one of the worst I've ever seen in a video game, and the truly repugnant escort mission towards the end. While this game was pretty outstanding the first few times I played through it, revisiting it for a third time only made me realize how flawed it really is, and how much better this style of game has been done since its release.

[h1] Ammo and Hacking [/h1]
I suppose that I may be a stickler for ammo consumption but even on difficulty settings where ammo is sparse, I feel like a  game should have a good logic system so that at any point in time the player isn't run out of ways to attack. At several points in time during my play-through (and it could have been at the highest difficulty) I found myself with no eve, no ammo, and only my wrench (which does fuck for all later on in the game). That's bad logic, I was struggling even when using ammo properly and buying ammo. Either I had no funds, no ammo, or both. That sucks and ruins the immersion and causes all combat to be broken every couple of seconds to switch ammo, or gun, or plasmid, or weapon hand, or just straight up contemplate how much longer you're willing to put up with this bullshit. Then we have more serious issues. Hacking. Hacking is an integral part of some games, Bioshock included. Most games require a mini-game or some sort of quick time event for the hacking to be successful. Something that breaks the immersion to further develop game-play mechanics. Sometimes hacking can be fun and introduce new things like with Nier Automata or System Shock. Bioshock gives the player the opportunity to mull over what the engineering capabilities might be in an underwater city that uses hydro-mechanics to engineer mechanical power sources. I think that's cool. The pressure goes through the system and allows the player to find ways to reroute power (or water in this case) in order to successfully hack. This would be great if the game had good logic, but so many times have I seen a hack unable to be completed because the game doesn't provide proper parts, has too many blockades, or just outright has unwinnable conditions. This all breaks immersion in a bad way, causing me and others to have to replay over and over and over until a winnable condition. That is just straight-up shitty game design. If you don't think the player should be able to hack everything, don't make everything hackable. Easy. The rest is just annoying, plus the game punishes you when you fail, by either damage or alarm. Each just means the removal of more resources and sometimes death.

Game Review: BioShock
Score: 2/10 - An Ideological Assault Disguised as Entertainment

BioShock presents itself as a thrilling narrative experience set in the underwater utopia of Rapture, but beneath its surface lies a relentless barrage of liberal ideology that aggressively undermines traditional American family values. This critically acclaimed title is nothing short of an ideological weapon, promoting a worldview that glorifies individualism while systematically dismantling the very principles that hold families and communities together.

A Relentless Push of Liberal Ideology
From the moment players descend into the depths of Rapture, they are bombarded with a narrative steeped in the philosophy of objectivism and libertarian ideals, which are often masked as high-minded discussions on freedom and choice. However, what BioShock fails to recognize is that unchecked individualism and an obsession with personal gain lead to societal decay. The game’s premise, which champions self-interest above all, echoes a distinctly liberal agenda that prioritizes the individual over the community.

Throughout the game, players encounter characters and factions that embody the extremes of these ideologies. The anarchic environment of Rapture is a testament to the dangers of a system that allows for the absolute freedom of the individual at the expense of social cohesion. This relentless focus on personal power and autonomy directly contradicts the values that have traditionally fostered strong family units, such as sacrifice, cooperation, and mutual support.

Undermining Traditional Family Values
BioShock not only promotes a hollow version of freedom but also actively assaults the very foundations of American family values. The narrative’s descent into chaos and moral ambiguity reflects a troubling disdain for the ideals of loyalty and commitment that have historically strengthened family bonds. The characters in Rapture are often depicted as self-serving and morally bankrupt, showcasing a world where personal gain trumps familial loyalty.

Moreover, the game presents relationships as transactional and manipulative rather than supportive and nurturing. The emphasis on betrayal and self-interest leaves little room for the love and respect that are vital to healthy family dynamics. By painting a picture of a world where individuals are isolated in their pursuits, BioShock encourages players to view relationships through a cynical lens, reinforcing the notion that traditional family structures are obsolete or irrelevant.

Conclusion: A Disturbing Message Wrapped in an Engaging Package
While BioShock is often lauded for its rich storytelling and immersive world, it ultimately serves as a disturbing critique of American values. The relentless promotion of liberal ideologies and the undermining of family structures position it as a dangerous piece of entertainment that leaves a lasting impact on its audience.

In an era where media can shape perceptions and influence beliefs, BioShock stands as a glaring example of how even the most celebrated games can perpetuate narratives that erode the very fabric of society. If you’re seeking a game that celebrates traditional values, community, and the importance of family, BioShock is a journey best left unexplored.

[h1] Masterful showcase of atmosphere, covered in mediocrity.	[/h1]

Bioshock is not terrible and if Steam had the option I'd give it a neutral rec. Hearing this game was supposed to be a spirtual successor to System Shock, one of the best FPS series of all time, and the fact that people talked about it like it was the second coming of Jesus Christ, I was hyped to play it. Unfortunately by the time I finished the game it ultimately left a bad taste in my mouth.

First off, Bioshock is one of the best examples of atmopshere in a video game I've played. You actually believe you're in Rapture, the infamous city at the bottom of the sea. The game uses a great selection of music and architecture to give you a strong old world vibe that delivers with great success. The soundtrack itself can be oppressive and lonely, adding further definition to the setting.

As much as I hate to say it though, that's really all I can say that I genuinely liked about Bioshock. The reasons for why I'm not entranced by it as everyone else has been for years is for a number of reasons. To not immediately come off as an over-privileged buffoon I'll start with the obvious technical issues that both the original and remastered versions of the game suffer from.

I actually started off playing the remastered version of Bioshock, but its numerous technical issues that I find outweigh that of the orginal made me instead play that version. Quite [b] shocking	[/b] because you'd figure a remaster would be better technically than the game it is trying to improve and modernise. As if it were set to an imaginary clock, multiple times the remaster crashed around every hour and a half or so, whilst deleting any saves I made during the specific session that had resulted in the crash, which meant I had to backtrack from waaay-back saves, which was pretty soul-crushing when it first happened.

Besides technical problems, the gameplay was my biggest dislike throughout the game. In my opinion the enemies are not nearly as varied as they should be. You mainly have Splicers and some different versions of them, such as Nitro Splicers, Spider Splicers, and more. While they're all slightly different in how you have to react to them, they all basically amount to the same, "Shoot and strafe until dead," strategy that gets extremely repetitive after a while. Even the Big Daddies, the game's iconic poster boy, are little more than slightly tougher foes that you simply have to put more bullets into while being slightly more careful. I feel as if the the Big Daddies and the rest of the cast of enemies could've had more focus in the way of interesting combat interactions rather than just serving as generic bullet sponges that get progressively more annoying through the game. There's also little to no feedback on the damage you do to enemies, which can be confusing since you might not be able to tell if you're actually hitting what you're aiming at or not.

Carrying on the idea of progession, while the enemies are fine at the beginning, it gets much, [i] much	[/i] less engaging as you play. The more you play the more you notice how blatantly repetitive the game's design gets. Particularly around six hours in, the enemies hit total rock bottom and become unbelievable bullet sponges that can take an egregious amount of shotgun shells point blank and still not die. Combat encounters were no longer a challenge so much as they were just an annoying chore to work through. It really doesn't help either when they constantly respawn in areas you've already cleared, making level exploration legitimately headache-inducing.

While it might seem like this puts you up against unfair odds- it doesn't. Even normal mode is way too lenient on the player, and it was rare that I died to anything. When I say this I don't even mean the Vita checkpoints that everybody (including fans) agrees there's too many of- I mean that the game just hands you too many resources in the first place. A lot of the time, instead of a tense survival horror-esque experience, it's an unengaging cakewalk to the next objective.

To add more outside of frustratingly unrefined FPS gunplay though, Bioshock has an interesting system called Plasmids. Plasmids are basically powers you can use to electrocute, ignite, or control enemies. There are many different plasmids in the game that you can use that all that do different things, but ultimately, you'll never feel the need to use more than the three basic ones: shock, fire, and telekinesis, which is a shame because the plasmids system has the potential to offer much more balance to the game if you actually needed to rely on them more to gather supplies for example.

Despite the game being called Bioshock, the game never utilizes the mechanic potential of water. While you can use it in conjunction with electric plasmids to shock enemies, the game never even tries anything more than that. I can think of so many ways in which water could've been implemented and made for really unique content. Again, I can't help but feel Bioshock totally missed out on the awesome potential it had with stuff like this.

Speaking of lost potential, the horror aspect of this game is never really met either. There's an attempt at it in the beginning when you first enter Rapture but never much again. 90% of this is due to the fact that the gameplay problems said earlier become more present the more you play but even then I feel like the focus could've been a little better put on that aspect. The oppressive setting and atmosphere of being alone in a city at the bottom of the ocean is directly in conflict with the unsatisfying gameplay.

There's more game design-related frustrations and all that could be put here, but the point's been made and the story is the other thing that deserves a look. Bluntly, I don't think the story is anything ground-breaking. I was disappointed by the slightly predictable twist that comes about 80% through the game, but the more I thought about it the more I started to appreciate it. What at first appears to be a predictable twist actually highlights a detail about the nature of games as a medium. I really recommend taking a look at stuff online if you've already played the game to see what I mean. Even with that said however I don't count myself a big fan of the story overall, as that twist is really it's only strong point.

Specifically, the ending feels rushed. One minute you're in the final room then the next you're immediately at the title screen, thinking, "that was it?" I got the good ending which I thought was a little too cheery and happy considering everything that you went through to get there. What remains after the ending are a lot of questions. What happened to Rapture? What happened to the poor people living in Rapture that have gone incurably insane? What happened to all of the ADAM? I feel even with the audio logs I listened to, things were still left unclear.

My expectations for Bioshock were pretty much destroyed as I played through it. I felt pretty frustrated from the mediocre gameplay and the fact that there was a heck of a lot of great potential missed. The story, while alright, still didn't really save the experience for me either. While I'm glad I got to experience one of the most beloved games of all time I'm also sad of the fact that I seemed to have played a vastly different experience than everyone else. Who knows, maybe it was all the hype that ruined it, or maybe I simply didn't get it. Either way, I'll definitely remember Bioshock not as a worthy sucessor to System Shock but more so as a thorn to the vision of a groundbreaking underwater FPS I still have stuck in my head.

At first, Bioshock amazed me. The opening is very well done, the music just clicks with the amazement of any player looking at the wonder that is Rapture as first seen. The setting is fantastic at first: A utopia, as considered by the city's founder, would only be viable underwater in the middle of the pacific. And the buildings and neon lights, like a 60s city, but with whales and fish swimming around, reinforced glass tubes connecting the buildings... It's fantastic. And then, you start entering a building, and hear cries of distress: the inhabitants monitoring new arrivals didn't expect you, or anyone to arrive. And as you stop, someone tries to get to you and help you, they're killed by a mutated woman, with hooks instead of hands. 

She disappears, and slowly through the first level of the game, so did my amazement and wonder. One of the tubes connecting buildings has its glass broken and starts leaking while you're on it, but it doesn't convey a sense of distress. You kind of have the feeling that the water is barely rising so that any idiot can escape the tube. (Also, the pressure on the seabed would probably do a lot more damage.) The first plasmid (a genetic modification that reflects in magic, in this case Force Lightning) just feels like a basic attempt at emergent gameplay, and it's the best plasmid: You can stun splicers (mutated humans) and insta-kill them with a wrench, at least on the first levels, or temporarily disable turrets and other robotics to hack them and turn them against their allies. It's nice, but could have been used better, and the other plasmids are either mostly useless or the emergent gameplay created from them is more basic than this one: oil + fire, and ice + shatter foes with crossbow, basically.

Gunplay is pretty weak: the projectile speed for the machine gun doesn't feel right, the pistol is pretty much a Half-Life 2-like pistol that has a ridiculous recoil yet doesn't feel good, the shotgun is kinda meh, etc. The enemy variety is very low: There's turrets, whether stationary or flying on helicopters, 5 kinds of splicers that, even though they behave differently, they look pretty much the same and scream the same deranged stuff. Finally, there are the Big Daddies. They come in two flavors: Bouncer, who rushes at you like a bull, and Rosie, who will kick your ass with a proximity mine launcher. They feel good at the first times, but then you realize their HP is severely bloated and that's mostly why they're hard. But you keep on doing that because, whle you have a choice, it's much more beneficial to just kill them instead of ignoring them (they will ignore you unless you get too close to them or the Little Sisters.) There are no new enemies after the first third of the game or so, only elite versions with even more HP bloat.

The level design would be good if the objectives weren't so annoyingly placed. At least 7 of the 12 levels (not counting the first one or the final boss) consist of you being led to a nearby objective to keep going to the next level, find out the objective is blocked and you have to unlock it by exploring the entire level. It just feels wrong. The levels are "kinda open-ended" but with linear objectives, and in some cases ist's annoying as hell to get to an objective, backtrack to an area you were previously in and then, only then, to have to go through where you have just gone to, but farther into the level. With respawning enemies this just turns into a massive pain in the ass, and it's just you traversing through the same stuff 4 times.

The presentation is very good, the 50s art-deco style is very well presented. As for the story: It has some nice biopunk stuff, but it's pretty much about the plot twist, part of which they decide to shove in your face and make it obvious a few hours before and the other part a pleasant surprise: [spoiler] You're not playing Bioshock, Bioshock is making you play it.[/spoiler] After the plot twist halfway through, well, the game should have ended right there. The quality takes a nosedive into a pretty underwhelming final boss (though, underwhelming final bosses exist in most FPSs I've played so far) and an ending that depends on a certain choice: This choice makes you Jebus Lord and Saviour or LITERALLY WORSE THAN HITLER. It's even worse that Dishonored at that.

Buy it on sale, I guess?
