BioShock, released in 2007, stands as a landmark title in the first-person shooter genre, praised for its atmospheric setting, gripping narrative, and innovative gameplay mechanics. Set in the dystopian underwater city of Rapture, the game offers a unique blend of narrative-driven exploration and fast-paced combat. However, the progression system, currency mechanics with many vending machiens, and its repetitive combat are points of contention among players and that I particularly disliked.

BioShock's greatest strength lies in its atmospheric design and stunning graphics. The underwater city of Rapture is a visually captivating and immersive environment, filled with intricate details that showcase the downfall of a utopian dream. The art deco architecture, flickering neon lights, and murky underwater vistas contribute to an unparalleled sense of place, creating a world that feels both haunting and alluring.

While BioShock's narrative is often lauded for its depth and twists, the utilization of audio logs falls short when compared to its spiritual predecessor, System Shock. System Shock adeptly integrated audio logs to provide context, world-building, and character development. In BioShock, while audio logs exist, their impact feels diminished, failing to create the same level of engagement or emotional connection with the characters and the unfolding story. Sometimes they add to world-building, sometimes they are required to progression, but this lack of consistency makes its use ambiguous and not as impactful as it was in the past. The narrative tries to be smart, but fails at the beginning to make you care about the protagonist. It feels pushed down your throat from the first time you leave the bathysphere.

One of BioShock's divisive aspects is its progression system, particularly the myriad vending machines and multiple currencies. The game introduces various upgrade options scattered across different machines, leading to a fragmented and confusing experience for players. With separate currencies for weapons, plasmids, and health, the system feels unnecessarily convoluted, hindering the flow of gameplay and diminishing the sense of accomplishment when obtaining upgrades. The fact you can only change your upgrades on a fresh playthrough might be a reason for some players to experiment with different builds, but for me just means I missed on a lot of content based on my upgrade path.

BioShock attempts to diversify combat through the introduction of plasmids, genetic modifications that grant the protagonist unique abilities. While initially intriguing, the combat system falls victim to repetitiveness. The limited number of plasmids and their predictable combinations result in encounters that become formulaic and lose their excitement over time. Despite the promise of varied combat, players may find themselves resorting to the same tactics repeatedly, detracting from the overall experience, without mentioning the limited amount of enemy types and clunky mechanics like research that completely kill the combat flow.

In conclusion, BioShock, with its captivating atmosphere, compelling narrative, and innovative setting, stands as a landmark title in gaming history. However, the game falters in its progression system, convoluted currency mechanics, and the repetitive nature of its combat. While the graphics and atmospheric design contribute to an unforgettable gaming experience, the missed opportunities with audio logs and the flawed progression system prevent BioShock from reaching its full potential. Some might say BioShock remains a must-play for those who appreciate immersive storytelling and atmospheric world-building in the realm of first-person shooters. I say there are better ways of spending 12-18 hours gaming.

The beginning of Ken Levine's console driven spiritual sucessor to one of the greatest games ever created for the PC. Irrational played it safe and decided that since almost nobody in the console crowd at the time would have ever heard of System Shock 2 that they could simply lift nearly every single plot element and gameplay mechanic from that game while simplifying it for consoles and then import it into their new game and nobody would be the wiser. Foor all intents and purposes it seems to have worked. When a game is a "spiritual sucessor" you can just jack everything and repaint it a new color.

In place of Shock2's psionics are the plasmids, in place of hybrids are splicers, in place of SHODAN is Fontane, and in place of cyber modules it's ADAM. 

Bioshock was a highly regarded game inspite of being almost completely unoriginal. Which isn't to say it isn't a playable game, yet it's clear that it was built more with the consoles in mind rather than a PC, mouse controls are never quite right and between each save load or level transition one must wait for whatever personal sensitvity settings you've placed the mouse at to "kick back in" if you've adjusted them from the defaults at all and I most certainly did.

The psionics/plasmids are not too terrible a trade off since half of Shock2's psi abilites end up being skipped over by veterans while most of the plasmids in Bioshock serve some function for the various playstyles a person may choose to adopt in Bioshock. However gunplay and firearms are rather weak and almost entirely propped up by the research, weapon upgrades, and the tonic system. 

One must research the various monsters roaming the city of Rapture to gain advantage of them, often not a big deal as you simply snap photos while being shot at. The real problem comes from needing to keep the very best tonics for your methods of dealing damage and finding all the upgrade machines located in the city while accepting the fact that some weapons are simply more efficent at dealing damage than others. The ability to craft addtional special ammo also helps make up some of the difference at the health and damage of enemies continues to upscale throughout the game and while you can buy newer versions of plasmids it's often better to wait until the third and last version is available before spending any precious adam (an exploit fixed in Bioshock 2).

So at best the gameplay in Bioshock is often just average with the occasional fight against a Big Daddy in order to get a Little Sister for more ADAM breaking up the monotony and even those are trivialized by the Vita Chambers that can bring you back again and again for no penality unless you shut them off (added in a later patch). 

Little Sisters are also where the much touted big moral choice comes into the game, a simple yes or no choice to rescue what's suppose to be a little girl. The problem with Bioshock is that all the human chracters look like cheap melted wax figures and not even close to human. So any attempt to dredge up empathy for me failed abysmally and I happily harvested every Little Sister on my first playthorugh. I later found out that the big moral choice leads to three endings, if you so much as harvest one sister you get the bad ending with a sad voice, if you harvest them all you get the bad ending with an angry voice and if you save them all you get the good ending, those deep moral choices I tell ya.

The plot fares no better since it's just literally System Shock 2's plotline all over again, running around Rapture doing chores for a guy you start to trust who turns out to be the actual big bad of the whole game who then tries to kill you once he has everything he wants. At the same time someone looked at the cover of Atlus Shrugged and decided it would help make the game deep and philisophical and I think the cover is about as far as they got. 

Bioshock is just a pale immitation of System Shock 2, but for a lot of people it's their first exposure to the "Shock" series even though it doesn't belong to it at all.

It's a challenging game with a couple twists on what calls itself a "shooter". The RPG elements are well-known, "plasmids" which give superpowers and the ability to upgrade weapons and craft items. 

The game is buggy and has design flaws.

Critisisms:
-EVE which powers plasmids, runs out very quickly, and ammo is sparse, so you might be down to a wrench to smack super-soldiers with. "EVE Saver" doesn't help much.
-Objects like turrets and cameras can be hacked, but sometimes the hack is impossible geometrically, which is very frustrating, especially considering the punishment to hacking: you get zapped and damaged and/or alarms set off and robots attack you for a full minute, which is a bit too long.
-The game is a bit long, with a lot of running around the same areas over and over again.
-The plotline is very complicated, even granting that it's meant to be so.
-Targetting: the targetting system for NPCs is very flawed. Allies will only attack an enemy after they've been attacked by you (which ruins the point of an ally), or they've already attacked you. 
-Buggy: there are interface bugs which can become very frustrating, for example, every time you get a new plasmid, the slots are mixed up, so in fast-paced combat, you can easily fire the wrong plasmid and die as a result. When you assign a new plasmid, it offsets others and mixes the slots. FIX: cycle through each slot, placing a dummy plasmid in a slot, then the appropriate one for each slot sequentially, this usually places them in the right spot.

Good parts:
-Low penalty for death: you revive at half life, half EVE to a nearby Vita station, within which you cannot be attacked. So how challenging this game is is diffused by dying not being a huge set-back.
-Challenging: enemies move unnaturally and turrets will kill you very quickly. A bit of critisism in that the turrets seem to kill you way faster than others.
-Good storyline: the narritive is interesting and suspenceful, while overly complicated. Some big moments in the plot are a bit unsatisfying, but arguably for narritive reason.

Minor things:
-Gatherer's Gardens and Gene Banks need to be one thing, expecially with the bug of slotting, where if you buy and slot a new plasmid it screws the hotkeys up until you can find a gene bank.
-RESCUE THE GIRLS, DON'T HARVEST.

So, I think it's time to completely re-edit my review and make it clearer. Third time's a charm, right? I realize the previous iterations weren't all that good at getting the point across. So now, I'll make it clear why, exactly, I don't recommend this game. The short version is, its story (its main selling point) is weak, lackluster and ends in the most generic way I could probably think of. Its gameplay is below average, though I won't fault it too much for that, the game's twelve years old. There's a serious lack of character interaction. And the only redeeming quality is represented by the environments, which are, well, decent. 

Now, the long version. 

Welcome to Rapture. You are a guy who ends up in a plane crash right next to the entrance into Rapture, the underwater anarcho-capitalist utopia created by a very rich guy. However, as you descend into it, you soon discover that the Eden it once was became something akin to hell. 

And here comes my very first complaint: The lack of character interaction. 

From the very beginning, you are guided by voices. Radio, recordings. There is a serious lack of character interaction, and it very easily gets tiring to just listen to characters you've never met. Recordings are supposed to tell the story of how the city turned into such a ruin, but only a bunch of them do that. The rest are just random characters talking about totally unrelated things. To make matters worse, tapes seem to appear at random, and if you've already cleared a room and moved out of it, you never know if another tape might pop up into it, causing you to miss it. The game hardly ever requires you to come back to the same room twice. And never to the same level. And let's be real now, did every freaking person in Rapture carry a tape recorder and tapes with them to record and throw about? It just doesn't make any sense. 

The gameplay, itself, is an endless stream of "fetch this" "kill this guy" "fetch that" "go here" "go there" and so on. I will choose not to fault it too much for that, it's an older game. Still, they could've been a little creative about it. 

Enemy variety: Splicers are your enemies. You have either splicers who use melee attacks, splicers who use guns, splicers who use hooks and splicers who use powers. That's it. And for being so few types, they sure are many because you can never catch a break. Much like the tapes, they appear in rooms you've already cleared once, and well, anywhere else for that matter. And then you have Big Daddies. 

They are definitely the most annoying type of enemies. Whether they like to charge at you or shoot at you, BDs are your worst enemies, provided you angered them. Worst part is that you'll have to fight quite a few, so stock up on everything because they don't go down all that easy. Some people find this challenging, but I say it's dreadful because they hardly have any kind of tactics. They just stomp you into the ground and that's it. 

And then, you get to the big twist. The big reveal that everyone seems to get wet about. 

"A man chooses, a slave obeys." It's by far the one statement that will be drilled into your head as you play, whether its via a tooltip message during loading screens or via the one man to whom the quote belongs. Well, I choose to detach myself from the hive mind that the game's fan base seems to be and state, loud and clear, that the big twist is nothing but a fart in the wind. To keep spoilers out, I won't say a thing about it, but don't expect fireworks. Don't expect anything, in fact, I did and I faced one of the worst disappointments I've felt with a game before. And what's even worse, the character whom I quoted makes the most nonsensical kind of choice I've ever been faced with. 

As for the morality-oriented storyline bit, well... aside from one choice related to morals which mildly affects the ending, that's about it. Don't go in expecting to be given too many choices or options. 

And in regards to the ending, well, I did not get to it. After being so disappointed with the supposedly peak moment of the game, I simply chose to not bother any longer, not waste any more time and read up on the ending. By this point I was expecting disappointment and it's good that I was, because the ending is a completely generic flop. It's like, at this point, they weren't even trying. 

Final verdict? I think it's pretty clear what I think about this game, but at the end of the day, the choice is yours. Just be warned, don't expect too much of it or you'll be disappointed.

Okay so this review is coming from someone who isn't blinded by nostalgia and played this game for the first time in 2022. For whatever reason, I never played this game when it originally came out, so I finally decided to pick it up on a steam sale for $4.99 and give it a go. For that price, I'd say pick it up if you've never played a bioshock game before, just don't expect too much. To me, the game feels very outdated, and its just not very enjoyable 15 years after its release. The best way I can describe it is that it feels very tedious. The combat isn't very fun, and you have to constantly upgrade your weapons and attributes or else all the enemies will quickly become annoying bullet sponges and it takes forever to kill them. The big daddies in particular are a huge pain. The problem is that the combat ends up just feeling like a chore, because you progress so fast in this game that you have to constantly keep upgrading.

The level design is very imaginative and pretty to look at, but it gets very repetitive and there isn't much variety. Normally games like this will have an engaging story to provide an incentive for the player to keep chugging away through the repetitive gameplay and environments, however there isn't much story here. Well, there's is but its all told through hundreds of audio logs which are scattered about the map, which again feel like a chore to listen to, not to mention its hard to hear over constant gunfire. So for most of this game you'll just be wondering around trying to complete some vague tasks while shooting the same 3 or 4 bad guys along the way. It's just not much fun or engaging.

Another problem I had was that I was constantly running out of ammo after killing like 3 guys, and its really annoying having to run around the map all the time and searching every cabinet and body for 3 pistol rounds. Then switching weapons in combat was a pain because each gun has multiple types of ammo, and it doesn't auto switch so you have to remember to switch ammo mid fight, which I found quite irritating.

So to summarize, the concept of Bioshock is very cool and iconic in the gaming industry, but unfortunately the story is rather lackluster, along with the generic characters, and the gameplay is very outdated. It's not a bad game, but I'm giving it a negative review to counteract the 94% user rating a bit. To me, this game is at best a 7/10, but in terms of my personal enjoyment, I might give it a 5.5/10.
